item.title: Police recover German tourist’s stolen laptop, bag in Natore
item.description:
Police have recovered a laptop and a bag containing valuables stolen from German national Kirill Lander Weber at Natore Railway Station.
Superintendent of Police Mohammad Shariful Haque confirmed the matter on Sunday.
The items were recovered from Noor Garments, a shop in the Nicha Bazar area of Natore town, around 8pm on Sunday, reports Bangla Tribune.
On Wednesday, Kirill travelled by train to Natore via Santahar after visiting several heritage sites in Bogura. At Natore Railway Station, a young man wearing a yellow vest approached him, claiming to be a railway employee, and gained his trust through conversation.
Kirill left his bag with the man in the station’s waiting room before going to an ATM booth to withdraw money and buy a ticket for a train to Darshana. When he returned, both the man and his bag were missing.
The bag contained a laptop, a DSLR camera and other valuables. Kirill had planned to enter India through the Gede border crossing after reaching Darshana.
Following the incident, police collected CCTV footage from the station and identified the suspect. Teams from Natore district police, railway police, Special Response Battalion (SRB-5) and Rajshahi Metropolitan Police subsequently launched efforts to arrest him and recover the belongings.
Earlier, officials said the investigation was complicated by the absence of a trackable mobile phone in the stolen bag, making it difficult to locate the suspect.
SRB-5 had also announced a reward for information leading to the suspect’s identification and arrest. On Saturday night, the unit put up posters featuring the suspect’s image at key locations around Natore Railway Station after analysing CCTV footage.
Hafiz Al Asad, commander of SRB-5’s Natore camp, confirmed the reward announcement and said efforts to arrest the suspect were continuing.

item.title: Sobhana’s historic ton in vain as Australia seal ODI series
item.description:
Sobhana Mostary struck a record-breaking century but Bangladesh Women suffered a nine-wicket defeat against Australia in the second ODI in Brisbane on Sunday, as the hosts chased down 221 with 131 balls to spare to take an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match series.
Sobhana scored 118 off 134 balls, hitting 18 fours, to register the highest individual score by a Bangladesh batter in women’s ODIs. Her remarkable innings rescued the visitors from a disastrous start and helped them post 220 for six after losing three wickets for just eight runs.
However, Georgia Voll’s unbeaten 131 off 97 balls and Phoebe Litchfield’s 70 off 51 deliveries powered Australia to 222 for one in just 28.1 overs, extending their winning streak at Allan Border Field to 23 matches.
Bangladesh’s innings appeared to be heading for an early collapse as Megan Schutt and Kim Garth dismantled the top order. Fargana Hoque fell for a 13-ball duck, Sarmin Sultana scored five and Sharmin Akhter departed without scoring, leaving the visitors in deep trouble inside eight overs.
Sobhana, however, responded with remarkable composure and attacking intent. Joining captain Nigar Sultana Joty, she gradually took control of the innings, finding boundaries against both pace and spin while Joty provided support at the other end.
The pair added 195 runs for the fourth wicket, the highest women’s ODI partnership at the Brisbane ground, transforming Bangladesh’s position and frustrating the Australian bowlers.
Sobhana reached her maiden ODI century off 123 balls before eventually falling to Schutt in the 48th over. Her 118 surpassed Bangladesh’s previous highest individual score in women’s ODIs and marked a significant milestone for the team against the world’s top-ranked side.
Joty remained unbeaten on 74 off 114 balls, striking seven fours, as Bangladesh finished on 220 for six. Schutt was Australia’s most successful bowler, claiming four wickets for 36 runs.
The visitors, however, had little answer to Australia’s aggressive chase. Voll and Litchfield added 162 runs for the opening wicket in just 19.5 overs, taking the game away from Bangladesh before Litchfield fell for 70.
Voll continued unabated, reaching her third ODI century before guiding Australia home alongside Ellyse Perry, who finished unbeaten on 19.
Despite the defeat, Sobhana’s historic innings offered Bangladesh a significant individual milestone, even as the team’s struggle to contain Australia’s batting underlined the gap they must bridge to compete consistently against the world’s leading sides.
Brief Score
Australia 222 for 1 (Voll 131*, Litchfield 70, Akter 1-32) beat Bangladesh 220 for 6 (Mostary 118, Nigar 74*, Schutt 4-36) by nine wickets

item.title: Hasan’s hat-trick puts Bangladesh in command
item.description:
Hasan Mahmud scripted history with a maiden hat-trick by a Bangladesh pacer in Test cricket and became the fastest Bangladeshi to 50 wickets in the format as the visitors strengthened their grip on the one-off Test against Afghanistan in Abu Dhabi on Sunday.
Bangladesh reached 223-6 in their second innings at stumps on the third day at Sheikh Zayed Stadium, extending their overall lead to 329 runs after bowling Afghanistan out for 240.
Hasan, who claimed five wickets for 55 runs, delivered a decisive burst in the morning session, removing Ismat Alam, Qais Ahmad and Zia-ur-Rehman in three consecutive deliveries in the 83rd over to become only the third Bangladeshi bowler to take a Test hat-trick.
Leg-spinner Alok Kapali had claimed Bangladesh’s first Test hat-trick against Pakistan in Peshawar in 2003, while off-spinner Sohag Gazi achieved the feat against New Zealand in Dhaka in 2013.
Hasan’s achievement was particularly significant as Bangladesh’s pace attack continued to establish itself as a formidable force in Test cricket. He also reached the 50-wicket milestone in the format, underlining his growing importance to the national side.
“When you start bowling, you try to bowl upright, swing the ball and get wickets. I was just trying that and bowling across,” Hasan said after the day’s play.
“I’m very pleased to see this kind of moment in the morning. Yesterday, I got one wicket in the whole day, but I wasn’t nervous at all. I was looking forward. I just felt that I should bowl straight, that’s it, and let the ball do its job.”
Afghanistan had appeared well placed to build a substantial first-innings total, with captain Rahmat Shah anchoring the innings. Rahmat remained unbeaten on 105 off 216 balls, but received little support from the lower order as the hosts lost their last six wickets for just 29 runs.
Hasan’s hat-trick reduced Afghanistan to 220-8, and Ebadot Hossain completed the demolition by taking four wickets for 56 runs. Mehidy Hasan Miraz claimed the other wicket as Afghanistan were dismissed in 89.1 overs.
Bangladesh had earlier posted 346 in their first innings, with Tanzid Hasan Tamim scoring 83, Shadman Islam making 67 and Litton Das contributing 53.
The visitors initially struggled in their second innings, slipping to 53-3 after Shadman, Mominul Haque and Tanzid departed cheaply. However, Mushfiqur Rahim and captain Najmul Hossain Shanto steadied the innings with a 159-run fourth-wicket partnership.
Mushfiqur, who had been dismissed for a duck in the first innings, scored 81 off 148 balls, hitting nine fours. Shanto made a patient 82 from 191 deliveries before falling late in the day.
Bangladesh lost three wickets in the final 10 overs, including Mushfiqur and Shanto, but Litton remained unbeaten on five alongside Mehidy, who was yet to score.
Reflecting on the historic morning, Hasan credited his teammates for helping him make the right decisions during the hat-trick over.
“Credit to the captain and Litton Das for talking and chatting with each other. They corrected me, saying it was going to hit, so I could take the review,” he said.
Hasan also looked ahead to Bangladesh’s upcoming Test assignments, including the World Test Championship and the tour of South Africa.
“I just want to keep going like that always,” he said, adding that the team would continue to focus on bowling the right lengths and maintaining the same process.
With a 329-run advantage and four wickets remaining, Bangladesh are firmly positioned to dictate the final two days, while Afghanistan face a formidable challenge to save the Test.

Day 3
Bangladesh 346 and 223 for 6 (Shanto 82, Mushfiqur 81, Ahmadzai 2-42, Zia 2-55) lead Afghanistan 240 (Rahmat 105*, Mahmud 5-51, Ebadot 4-56) by 329 runs

item.title: UN, EU leaders slam Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
item.description:
UN and EU leaders voiced shock on Sunday at an attack by Yemen's Houthi rebels on an airport in Saudi Arabia and warned against an escalation in the deadly conflict.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by Saturday's attack on Riyadh's airport, which killed 12 people and wounded over 300, according to aviation authorities.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately," Guterres said in a statement.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen called the attack a "dangerous escalation" and said the Iran-backed group must halt strikes on civilian targets.
"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwave sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
"These murderous attacks at civilians must stop at once," she said, adding the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia".
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he "firmly condemns" the attack, which he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he wrote on X.
Meanwhile, UK Defence Minister Wes Streeting said the attacks were "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation".

item.title: Why should the public pay the ‘penalty’ for rescuing banks?
item.description:
No government can escape responsibility for the looting of the banking sector. However, the previous Awami League government stands in a class of its own. The looting took place with every form of state patronage, while Bangladesh Bank failed spectacularly in its role as regulator. The central bank approved all kinds of wrongdoing to accommodate the demands of the government of the day.

As a result, the volume of non-performing loans (NPLs) in the country now exceeds Tk 6 trillion, accounting for 32.78 per cent of total loans. As much as 72 per cent of these bad loans are concentrated in just 10 banks.

Taken together, Bangladesh now has the highest rate of loan defaults in the world. Bangladesh Bank must bear responsibility for this.

Yet the governor of that very central bank is now saying that public money was embezzled and that the public must pay to cover the losses. In the words of Governor Mostaqur Rahman, the public will have to pay a penalty. He has even provided an estimate of the amount, and it is substantial. Speaking at an event last Saturday, he said Tk 600 billion would have to be spent every year to recover from the collapse of the banking sector. This would have to continue for the next five to eight years.

Over five years, the total cost would amount to Tk 3 trillion; over eight years, it would reach Tk 4.8 trillion. Compared with the budget for the 2026–27 fiscal year, the annual outlay would be equivalent to around 6.5 per cent of the budget.

The Bangladesh Bank governor has also offered comparisons to illustrate the scale of the expenditure. For instance, Tk 600 billion a year could be used to support 20 million families through family cards, or it could pay for the construction of two Padma Bridges.

Why should we pay the penalty?

According to the latest estimates from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), the penalty would amount to approximately Tk 3,432 per person, based on the country’s population.

The question is whether this money could be borrowed from a development partner instead of being taken from taxpayers. The answer is no. No development partner is likely to lend money to cover losses caused by looting in the banking sector.

We know that the World Bank has an ongoing lending programme for Bangladesh’s financial sector. The $450 million programme covers deposit protection, strengthening Bangladesh Bank’s supervisory capacity and preparations for bank restructuring. In other words, the World Bank is not providing money to cover the losses themselves. The only source left, therefore, is taxpayers’ money.

It is to be remembered that development partners never lend without conditions. The money Bangladesh is receiving from the World Bank also comes with numerous conditions. If lenders impose conditions when providing loans, why should the public have to hand over their tax money in the name of a penalty without any conditions in return?

The questions, then, are simple: why should we pay this penalty, and what will we get in return?

How much political will does the government have?

The biggest question is how much political will the government actually has to put the banking sector in order. There are certainly reasons to be sceptical.

On 9 May 2025, the interim government promulgated the Bank Resolution Ordinance. It did not allow former bank owners to regain ownership. But the law subsequently passed by the BNP government in parliament included a new provision that opened the door for former owners to take control again.

Critics argued that the provision had been inserted specifically to facilitate the return of a controversial businessman. Following strong criticism, the provision was eventually scrapped. Development partners had also raised objections.

One of the most widely discussed problems under the previous government was the entrenchment of family control over private banks. The previous administration had enabled this to facilitate looting. The public expects family dominance in the banking sector not to return.

To that end, Bangladesh Bank proposed reducing the maximum number of directors from a single family from three to two, and cutting the maximum consecutive tenure of a director from 12 years to six. It has now emerged, however, that the Financial Institutions Division (FID) of the Ministry of Finance has rejected both proposals. Instead, it has proposed reducing the maximum consecutive tenure from 12 years to nine while retaining the existing rule allowing up to three directors from the same family.

Past experience has shown that governments have retained the Financial Institutions Division ostensibly to oversee the banking sector but in practice to impose political decisions on economic policymaking. The same pattern appears to be continuing.

Yet the BNP pledged in its election manifesto to establish a commission to reform the financial sector and abolish the Financial Institutions Division under the Ministry of Finance. Implementing these two pledges after coming to power would be a major test of the government’s political will.

Here, I would like to refer to a report prepared by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in 2019. The report, titled Financial Sector Stability Review, was never published because the Awami League government at the time was unhappy with its findings.

The IMF wrote: “There is a deep-rooted and persistent tendency among a section of society not to repay loans. Some influential and wealthy businesspeople have realised that the country lacks effective mechanisms to compel them to repay their loans.

Decision-making in Bangladesh’s financial sector has come under the control of influential borrowers. The situation is such that the default of just three large borrowers could cause a bank to fail.”

If that system is allowed to return, the public’s payment of the penalty will have been entirely in vain.

What mechanisms are in place to recover the money?

According to government figures, courts have ordered the seizure, attachment or freezing of assets worth approximately Tk 769.84 billion, both at home and abroad, as part of efforts to recover assets siphoned out of the country.

Of this amount, assets worth Tk 573.2593 billion are located in Bangladesh, while those held abroad are valued at Tk 196.58 billion.

We know that recovering assets held abroad is not easy. Various legal procedures must be completed. But most of the assets in question are located within the country. Recovering even these assets could provide some relief to the banking sector.

Simply announcing the formation of a task force will not reassure members of the public who are being asked to pay the penalty. They will want to see tangible progress.

Recovering losses alone will not strengthen banks

Bangladesh has so far merged five banks to form a new bank. Only time will tell whether this initiative succeeds. But mergers alone will not solve all the problems.

Malaysia, South Korea and several other countries offer examples of how to repair a weakened banking sector. The 1997 Asian financial crisis brought the banking sectors of several East Asian countries to the brink of collapse. Their recovery offers important lessons for Bangladesh.

Following the Asian financial crisis, Malaysia established Danaharta to acquire and manage non-performing loans, Danamodal to inject capital into banks, and the Corporate Debt Restructuring Committee to restructure the debts of large corporate borrowers.

At the same time, it consolidated its banking sector, reducing 51 banking institutions to 10 banking groups. In other words, it did not simply remove bad loans; it also changed banks’ capital structures and institutional framework.

During the crisis, South Korea closed several inefficient banks. The Korea Asset Management Corporation was tasked with acquiring non-performing loans. To maintain depositors’ confidence, the government temporarily guaranteed deposits held with financial institutions.

Earlier, during its banking crisis in the 1990s, Sweden established a dedicated bank support authority. It assessed the financial condition of distressed banks, injected capital into those that could be saved and took control of those that could not. Separate asset management companies, Securum and Retriva, were also established to handle impaired assets. The government published information on the condition of the banking sector and the assistance provided, making accountability an integral part of the programme.

The public has conditions too

When governments borrow from development partners, they must meet conditions attached to the loans and report on progress. The same requirements should apply when taxpayers’ money is used to rescue banks.

The government must clearly explain what reforms will be undertaken in return for this money, what results are expected, who will be held responsible if the reforms fail, and what punishment has been imposed on those responsible for the previous crisis.

The banking sector needs money to recover. But the public must also be shown how much the sector will change in return for that money.

item.title: 10 Dhaka–Riyadh flights cancelled after attack on Saudi airport
item.description:
Ten flights from Dhaka to Riyadh have been cancelled following a Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital. A total of 3,431 passengers were scheduled to travel on these flights.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) provided the information on Monday morning.

According to CAAB, the cancelled flights include two operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, two by US-Bangla Airlines, three by Saudia and three by Riyadh Air.

Identities of 26 Bangladeshis killed or injured in airport attack in Saudi Arabia confirmed

In a press release yesterday, Sunday, the state-owned airline said passengers would be informed of the revised schedules for its two cancelled flights at 12:00 pm Monday. Biman suspended flights BG 339 and BG 340 on Saturday night.

Following the attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday night, the airport suspended operations. This disrupted air connectivity between Dhaka and Riyadh. By Sunday, CAAB had reported the cancellation of eight flights from Dhaka, leaving 2,951 passengers stranded.

Updating its information on Monday morning, CAAB said the number of cancelled flights had risen to 10. The number of affected passengers had also increased.

Bangladesh condemns attack on Saudi airport, seeks details of victims

The attack on Riyadh airport has created uncertainty over flight operations. Passengers have been advised to contact their airlines to check the latest status of their flights.

According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, all flights bound for Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled.

A Reuters report said the decision followed attacks and explosions at the Saudi capital’s international airport.

Reuters reported the suspension of flights at Riyadh International Airport, adding that airport authorities had advised passengers to contact their respective airlines before travelling to the airport and to check the latest status of their flights.

item.title: What charges brought against Ayash, Marzia, under which sections?
item.description:
A court has remanded four people, including A N M (Al Nur Mohammad) Ayash, member-secretary of the State Dialogue Forum, over defacing wall art depicting Rabindranath outside the Shilpakala Academy in Segunbagicha, Dhaka.

The case against the four has been filed under Sections 120B, 153A and 295A of the Penal Code. If the charges are proved, the offences carry different terms of punishment under these provisions.

In its remand application, police accused the four of attempting to spread hatred and create divisions in religious sentiment and communal harmony ahead of the upcoming Durga Puja, as well as of criminal conspiracy and incitement to create disorder.

Legal experts say Section 120B of the Penal Code deals with criminal conspiracy. A case can be filed under this section against anyone accused of conspiring to commit an offence.

The punishment depends on the nature of the conspiracy and the penalty prescribed for the offence concerned. Conspiracy to commit a serious offence may carry the same punishment as abetting that offence. In other cases, the law provides for up to six months’ imprisonment, a fine, or both.

Section 153A of the Penal Code deals with promoting enmity between different groups. Spreading or attempting to spread enmity or hatred between different groups of citizens through words, writing, signs or visual representations constitutes an offence under this section. It carries a maximum penalty of two years’ imprisonment, a fine, or both.

Section 295A, meanwhile, deals with deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings. Insulting or attempting to insult the religion or religious beliefs of a group, through words, writing or visual representations, with the deliberate and malicious intention of offending its religious feelings constitutes an offence under this section. The maximum penalty is two years’ imprisonment, a fine, or both.

However, the filing of a case under these provisions does not mean that the accused have been found guilty. The court will determine the punishment in accordance with the law if the charges are proved.

On 5 October, Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) cleared footpaths in Segunbagicha of encroachments. Portraits of 10 eminent figures who made significant contributions to art, literature and culture—including Shilpacharya Zainul Abedin, Satyajit Ray, Rabindranath Tagore and Kazi Nazrul Islam—were subsequently painted on a wall beside the footpath.

Ayash drew public attention on 10 October when he attempted to erase the graffiti in Segunbagicha. He was previously the member-secretary of the Mymensingh metropolitan unit of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement. In recent times, however, he has courted controversy through a series of incidents.

Besides Ayash, 29, police showed Mohammad Sakibul Hasan, 19, Mohammad Sujon Mia, 18, and Marzia Khandaker Rimi, 27, as arrested in the case yesterday, Sunday.

Police sought 10 days of remand for all four accused for the sake of the investigation.

Defence lawyer Monir Hossain told the court that the allegations against the four did not warrant imprisonment. “The matter could have been settled with a slap. Remand is out of the question,” he said.

The court, however, ordered remand for different periods. Ayash and Sakibul were remanded for three days each, while Sujon and Marzia were remanded for two days each.

Asked for comment, Omar Faruqui, the state counsel and public prosecutor (PP) at the Dhaka Metropolitan Sessions Judge’s Court, told Prothom Alo: “Their actions amount to a kind of declaration of war against the government. They have made statements at various times that hurt religious sentiments. They are undermining our culture of communal harmony. Through mob actions, they have created fear among people across the country.”

Faruqui further said their aim was to obstruct development and attract viral attention. “That is why they use abusive language. They try to incite religious tensions. We need to find out whether there is a network behind them,” he said.

item.title: CUET Shutdown: New VC breaks lock to enter office with Chhatra Dal leaders
item.description:
Amidst the ongoing student-led 'complete shutdown' at Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET), the newly appointed Vice-Chancellor (VC) Professor Shaikh Shariful Alam entered his office after breaking the padlock.

He entered the campus at around 9:00 am on Monday.

According to university sources, the VC arrived on campus in a HiAce microbus. At the main gate, he identified himself only as a ‘teacher’. He later went to the vice-chancellor’s office with Bangladesh Jatiotabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) leaders, breaking the lock on the entrance.

CUET VC withholds teachers’, officials’ salaries amid protests

During an on-the-spot visit to the VC building in the morning, he was seen sitting in the Vice-Chancellor's chair. CUET unit Chhatra Dal President Wasif Rashed, Joint General Secretary Abu Sufian Al Sabit and Organising Secretary Biplob Hossain were present in his room.

When asked, Abu Sufian Al Sabit told Prothom Alo, "We entered together."

Professor Shaikh Shariful Alam is a faculty member of the Electrical and Electronic Engineering Department at Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET). On 21 September, he was appointed as the VC of CUET, replacing Professor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem.

Why so much anger over vice-chancellor change at CUET

However, protesting the appointment and demanding Sayem’s reinstatement, students began a ‘complete shutdown’ the following day.

As part of the protest, they locked the entrance to the vice-chancellor’s office. Teachers, officials and staff have also been observing a work strike since that day with the same demand. As a result, classes and exams at CUET have remained suspended for 20 days.

Facing protests from teachers, students and staff, the new VC had not been able to enter the CUET campus until now. However, he officially assumed his duties on 24 September by sending his joining letter to the President and the secretary of the Ministry of Education.

item.title: 4 murders in Rangpur: Suspects’ DNA found on date seed, cucumber, towel
item.description:
DNA evidence from several items recovered at the scene of the murder of four members of a family, including retired teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, in Machhuapara, Rangpur city, has linked the two arrested suspects, Siddhartha Das and Mugdha Das, to the crime.

Investigators found Mugdha Das’s DNA on a date seed, Siddhartha Das’s DNA on a piece of cucumber, and both suspects’ DNA on a cigarette butt. They also identified only Mugdha Das’s DNA on a sample taken from the towel wrapped around the neck of victim Pritilata Chakraborty.

The Criminal Investigation Department’s (CID) forensic laboratory in Dhaka examined various samples collected from the crime scene. The DNA analysis report contains these findings.

Jinnat Ali, inspector of the Detective Branch (DB) of Rangpur Metropolitan Police and the investigation officer in the case, confirmed the information to Prothom Alo.

Inspector Jinnat Ali said, “An analysis of the DNA report, the recovered evidence, the suspects’ confessional statements and witnesses’ accounts has established Siddhartha and Mugdha’s involvement in the four murders. The DNA analysis found no evidence of anyone other than the four victims and the two suspects at the crime scene.”

He added that investigators had completed the investigation and would submit the charge sheet against the two suspects to the court within the next month.

Jinnat Ali spoke to Prothom Alo at the Rangpur Metropolitan Police Detective Branch office on Sunday afternoon. He provided details about the investigation, the forensic report and the motive behind the widely discussed quadruple murder.

Jinnat Ali said, “We received the DNA analysis report from the CID headquarters in Dhaka on Thursday.” He added that investigators had sent 31 types of samples collected from the crime scene to the CID forensic laboratory for testing on 31 August and 1 September.

The samples included a date seed, a piece of cucumber, a fruit-cutting knife, foil used for consuming yaba, a cigarette butt, stains from a washbasin and blood samples from the two suspects.

No evidence of rape found

Following the four murders, questions arose over whether Agami Chakraborty, daughter of Ganapati Chakraborty, and her mother, Pritilata Chakraborty, had been raped. To establish the facts, investigators sent vaginal swab samples from both women to the CID forensic laboratory for DNA testing.

However, the investigation officer said the report found no evidence of rape.

How the four victims were killed

The investigation officer outlined the role each suspect allegedly played in the murders after analysing the DNA report, the recovered evidence, the suspects’ confessional statements submitted to the court, testimony from four people who testified in court, and statements from 56 people who gave statements to the police.

According to Jinnat Ali, Siddhartha and Mugdha jointly killed Ganapati Chakraborty. Mugdha Das killed Ganapati’s wife, Pritilata Chakraborty. Siddhartha Das killed their college-going daughter, Agami Chakraborty. The two suspects jointly killed their 12-year-old son, Ayush Chakraborty.

item.title: Why is Pakistani politics revolving around a prisoner?
item.description:
PAKISTAN-POLITICS-PROTEST

Whether anyone accepts it or not, the truth is that Pakistan’s politics revolves around a man who has been imprisoned in Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail for the past three years. The name of this prisoner is Imran Khan. On 18 August, the Supreme Court of Pakistan ordered that Imran Khan be transferred to Al-Shifa Hospital in Islamabad within two days. Ignoring this order, Shehbaz Sharif’s government gave Imran Khan a tour of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) and locked him back up in Adiala Jail.

Sohail Afridi, Chief Minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, belongs to Imran Khan’s party, Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). Afridi announced a long march toward Islamabad for Imran Khan’s release. To stop the march, the federal government began negotiations with PTI. But Afridi said that if Imran Khan tells them to stop the long march, they will stop. The federal government did not agree. Holding Afridi responsible for the failure of the talks, it decided to impose Governor’s Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Governor’s Rule means the end of Afridi’s government, but the long march has not ended. On Sunday, Shehbaz Sharif convened a meeting of the federal cabinet, declared Afridi a facilitator of terrorists, and decided on Governor’s Rule and an emergency. Imposing Governor’s Rule in a province of Pakistan is nothing new, but the history attached to it is very painful. Sadly, this bitter history is being repeated again and again.

In 1954, when elections were held in East Pakistan (present-day Bangladesh), the Muslim League was defeated and A.K. Fazlul Huq of the United Front became chief minister. The federal government of Pakistan declared Fazlul Huq an enemy of the country, dismissed him, and imposed Governor’s Rule in East Pakistan through Iskander Mirza. In the 1970 elections, the Awami League won a majority. Instead of transferring power to the Awami League, the military dictator General Yahya Khan decided on a military operation.

First, Lieutenant General Sahabzada Yaqub Ali Khan was made governor and ordered to carry out the operation. When he refused, General Tikka Khan was made governor. Tikka Khan began the operation but could not establish peace, so General AAK Niazi was made governor, and he surrendered to joint forces and thus Bangladesh was born.

Even after Pakistan broke apart, the lessons of old mistakes were not learned. In 1973, the elected government of Balochistan’s Chief Minister Ataullah Mengal was dismissed and Governor’s Rule was imposed in the province. Akbar Bugti was made governor, but only ten months later he bid farewell to Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. In 1975, Hayat Muhammad Khan Sherpao, a close associate of Bhutto, was murdered at Peshawar University. Blaming Wali Khan and his associates for the murder, Governor’s Rule was imposed in the province.

Major General Syed Ghous, a former ISI officer, was made governor, but he could not handle the province’s situation. Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa stand today exactly where they stood fifty years ago. Akbar Bugti, who became governor in 1973, was declared a traitor by the Pakistani army in 2006 and was killed in the mountains of Balochistan. Ataullah Mengal and Wali Khan were declared facilitators of the country’s enemies.

And Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who made that declaration, was hanged at the gallows in 1979 at the hands of the Pakistani army.

Pakistan’s political history is very cruel. This history tells us that in 2018, Imran Khan, too, became prime minister riding on the shoulders of military generals. When differences arose with those generals, Imran Khan was removed from power and Shehbaz Sharif was seated in the prime minister’s chair.

The generals thought that, just as politicians like Nawaz Sharif had in the past struck deals after going to jail and gone to Saudi Arabia or Britain, Imran Khan too would not be able to spend long in jail. Like Nawaz Sharif, Imran Khan would make a deal and go abroad. But Imran Khan refused to become Nawaz Sharif.

Shehbaz Sharif’s government is not ready to take the risk of releasing him, and is not even ready to transfer him to a hospital. Had the Supreme Court’s 18 August decision been implemented, there would have been neither Governor’s Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa nor a long march.

Sohail Afridi’s long march is for Imran Khan’s release, but Shehbaz Sharif has also started a long march of his own. This long march is pushing Pakistan toward a civilian dictatorship.

The Shehbaz Sharif government’s position is that whatever they are doing, they are doing within the Constitution. The Constitution also commands them to implement the Supreme Court’s orders, but where the Constitution becomes an obstacle in their path, they ignore it. Where the Constitution serves the fulfillment of their political agenda, they become champions of the Constitution. Imran Khan used to do much the same.

Imran Khan jailed many of his political opponents, including Shehbaz Sharif, and kept a ban on an insolent journalist like me for nine months.

But there is one difference. In the Global Democracy Index, Imran Khan’s government was classified among Hybrid Regimes, but today Shehbaz Sharif’s government has been classified among Authoritarian Regimes.

Governor’s Rule and an emergency have been imposed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa at a time when Pakistan’s relations with India and Afghanistan are extremely tense. India has suspended the Indus Waters Treaty and begun new projects to divert the flow of Pakistan’s rivers. Terrorism is taking place in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan via Afghanistan.

Until a few months ago, Pakistan’s rulers were boasting proudly of their mediating role between America and Iran, because US President Donald Trump was praising them every day. Then Trump began direct negotiations with Iran.

Pakistan made a mutual defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey. The Pakistani government claims it will defend Saudi Arabia at all costs. By all means, let Saudi Arabia be defended, but Pakistan’s government should first put its own house in order.

In the Global Terrorism Index 2026, Pakistan has ranked first. To combat terrorism, Shehbaz Sharif’s government will have to unite all political forces. There must be no impression that, in the name of the war on terror, an operation is being carried out against one political party in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Such a policy will not bring peace to the province.

Shehbaz Sharif’s government has become a prisoner of Imran Khan phobia. This captive government has pushed Pakistan toward civilian dictatorship. This government needs to be freed from Imran Khan phobia and should learn a lesson from the fate of Bangladesh’s former prime minister, Sheikh Hasina.

*Hamid Mir is a Pakistani journalist who has survived several assassination attempts and faced repeated bans under successive governments.

item.title: Narendra Modi faces a tough challenge
item.description:
It has been less than a week since Narendra Modi completed 25 years in power. He served as chief minister of Gujarat for 13 consecutive years and has been at the helm of the country for the past 12.

Many people remain convinced that he will spend another three years as prime minister and lead his party and alliance into the next Lok Sabha election. Over this quarter-century, no figure has emerged, either within his party or among the opposition, who could outshine Modi.

Yet he is facing considerable uncertainty at this moment. His political fortunes, or perhaps the consequences of his own actions, have once again brought him face to face with a crucial test. The question is whether he will overcome it, as he has so often done before.

Over the past 25 years, Modi has faced no shortage of challenges and crises. Soon after becoming Gujarat’s chief minister in 2001, he had to deal with the devastating earthquake in Kutch.

The following year came the Godhra incident and the communal riots in Gujarat. He faced fierce criticism from senior leaders of his own party. When his position as chief minister was on the verge of collapse under the wrath of Atal Bihari Vajpayee, it was Lal Krishna Advani, then regarded as the BJP’s iron man, who came to his rescue.

The fallout from the Gujarat riots continued for years, both at home and abroad. He weathered the arrest of Amit Shah, his trusted right-hand man, cases related to the riots and the humiliation of having his US visa revoked.

Despite winning fewer seats in the 2024 election, Modi has not once allowed anyone to see how difficult it has been for him to run the government and keep his coalition intact over the past two years.

Gradually, he consolidated his position to such an extent that, ahead of the 2014 Lok Sabha election, the RSS put him forward as its trump card against the Congress. The rest is history.

Modi’s life as prime minister has hardly been free of turbulence. He brought trouble upon himself, perhaps without realising it, with his announcement of demonetisation.

The introduction of the goods and services tax (GST) also drew considerable opposition. Conflicts across the border kept him on edge. First came Uri, then Pulwama.

Despite failures in preventing the attacks, he demonstrated how adverse circumstances could be turned to political advantage. His victory in the 2019 Lok Sabha election, with an even larger majority, showed what a combination of hard-line Hindutva campaigning and election machinery could achieve.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, Modi supplied vaccines to several countries in the developing world, seeking to project himself as a global leader. Despite being shaken by Chinese aggression in Galwan, he managed to avoid losing his footing.

The farmers’ protests put him under pressure, but he was ultimately forced to withdraw the three controversial farm laws. He showed that he knew when to take a step back.

Despite winning fewer seats in the 2024 election, Modi has not once allowed anyone to see how difficult it has been for him to run the government and keep his coalition intact over the past two years.

Few political leaders in India have matched Modi’s ability to turn political setbacks into opportunities and emerge stronger from adversity.

Abhijeet Dipke among others to be produced before executive magistrate at Delhi today
Abhijeet Dipke, founder of Cockroach Janta Party, detained at Delhi Airport

Whether Modi can overcome this crisis, as he has previous ones, has suddenly become a question hanging over him. Serious allegations now confront the government: whether Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is conducting elections in accordance with the Constitution; whether the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls was carried out in compliance with the law; whether the Gyanesh-led Election Commission is being used to serve the BJP’s interests; and whether, despite wearing the mantle of impartiality, he is acting as a blind loyalist of Modi and Shah. Until now, every such allegation directed at the government has come from the opposition.

For the first time, however, two people who have reinforced the opposition’s questions and suspicions are colleagues of Gyanesh Kumar himself—people whose appointment was also made by Modi and Shah. Nearly three weeks have passed, yet Gyanesh Kumar and his team have not issued a statement dismissing The Indian Express report as false.

Delhi under siege

The three election commissioners have still not held a press conference to rebut the allegations. Instead, their press release has, by implication, suggested that every allegation raised by the newspaper is true.

This crisis differs from the earlier ones in several important respects. For the first time, the Election Commission, a constitutional body, has come under direct fire. The Modi government has reshaped the process for appointing its officials in ways that favour the ruling establishment.

Removing the Chief Justice of India from the committee responsible for appointing the chief election commissioner and election commissioners, and replacing him with another cabinet member, has made it clear that the government is determined to entrust the conduct of elections to its own “loyalists”.

The decision to grant the three commissioners lifelong legal protection is also unprecedented and controversial. The President, the prime minister and even the Chief Justice of India do not enjoy such immunity. Why, then, this protection? Whose interests does it serve? What wrongdoing by the Election Commission is the government seeking to shield through this immunity? These serious questions are stirring public debate, and the Modi government has yet to offer convincing answers. Both matters are currently under consideration by the Supreme Court.

Until now, the challenges confronting Modi have come from political parties, individuals, professional groups such as farmers, workers and physicians, or government employees.

For the first time, the country’s Gen Z has stood up to the government and challenged it directly. The sweeping changes brought about by Gen Z movements in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal are well known. Now, Gen Alpha has joined forces with this fearless generation.

After more than a decade in power, the policies and actions of the prime minister and his party have created a degree of political fatigue and disillusionment. Gen Z’s lack of trust in the government has also energised the opposition. The movement, however, has yet to develop a coherent structure, and the opposition remains far from united in its opposition to Modi.

Delhi paralysed, widespread arrests

The BJP has already decided to frame the struggle as one between “patriots and anti-nationals”, “nationalists and separatists”, and as a foreign conspiracy against the country. BJP president Nitin Nabin has made this position clear, claiming that foreign enemies who resent India’s progress under Modi are conspiring against the government. The contest, in the BJP’s framing, is therefore between true Indians and those opposed to India.

This is how Narendra Modi has prevailed for a quarter-century. He has built his electoral fortunes on hard-line Hindutva, invoking the “Hindustan-Pakistan” narrative. Now, for the first time, the Election Commission itself faces a fundamental challenge, with Gen Z raising questions about the state of democracy.

It is worth remembering that by 2029, India’s Gen Z population is projected to reach 380 million. If Gen Alpha is added, the two generations together will account for 800 million voters by the next Lok Sabha election. Can Modi overcome opposition from these generations by relying on Hindutva and promising good governance? Can he keep his head held high and defy all political speculation? There is little doubt that this may well be the greatest challenge of his political life.

item.title: Experts call for changes in engineering education to meet industry needs
item.description:
Experts believe Bangladesh must maintain and further improve the quality of its engineering education following the achievement of international recognition. They say university curricula must align with industry requirements and that students must develop practical problem-solving skills alongside theoretical knowledge. They have stressed the need for effective policies, improved teaching competencies, robust assessment systems and stronger collaboration between universities and industry.

These views emerged at a symposium on the role of policy support in accreditation to ensure the quality of engineering education, held at the Hotel InterContinental in Shahbagh, Dhaka, on Sunday. The event, titled “BAETE National Symposium 2026”, was organised by the Board of Accreditation for Engineering and Technical Education (BAETE), under the Institution of Engineers, Bangladesh (IEB). Engineering professors, experts and professional engineers from universities across the country attended the event.

“Standards must be maintained”

Megat Johari Megat Mohd Noor, a member of the Board of Engineers Malaysia and president of the Malaysian Society for Engineering and Technology, delivered a presentation at the symposium. He highlighted the importance of international accreditation in ensuring the quality of engineering education.

Megat Johari said, “Quality engineering education must equip students with technical knowledge, analytical skills and the ability to solve complex problems.” He added that curricula must also incorporate emerging technologies, innovation, ethics and lifelong learning.

According to Megat Johari, graduates’ competencies must align with industry requirements. To achieve this, he stressed the need for effective assessment systems, qualified teachers, engagement with industry and continuous improvement across educational institutions.

Lock Kai Sang, chair of the Washington Accord and a professor at the Singapore Institute of Technology, said, “Bangladesh became a full signatory of the Washington Accord in 2023.” He said the country must now build on this recognition to improve the quality of engineering education continuously across its universities.

He emphasised the need to clarify the authority and responsibilities of accreditation bodies, safeguard their independence and credibility, ensure adequate resources and strengthen teachers’ competencies. He also called for graduates’ competencies to remain aligned with the needs of national development.

Professor Lock said, “Accreditation must go beyond preparing documents and complying with regulations.” He stressed that assessors must evaluate, based on evidence, what students learn and the skills they acquire. The government, universities, accreditation bodies and industry must work together to ensure continuous improvements in educational quality.

BAETE Chairman Professor Tanvir Manzur highlighted the gap between university education and the practical demands of the engineering profession. He said, “University students acquire the theoretical knowledge they need, but they must also develop the ability to make decisions in real-world situations, solve problems, communicate effectively and work in teams.” He added that they must learn to work with incomplete information and within practical constraints.

Professor Tanvir’s presentation addressed issues such as coordination among engineers from different disciplines, software verification, construction quality control, regulatory compliance and cost considerations.

He said BAETE’s accreditation framework could help define curriculum outcomes, assess students’ ability to solve complex problems and strengthen engagement with industry. This would create opportunities to improve public safety and infrastructure quality, reduce dependence on foreign engineers and enhance the international recognition of Bangladeshi engineers.

Government to provide policy support

Mahdi Amin, an adviser to the Prime Minister, attended the afternoon session of the day-long symposium as the chief guest. Describing Bangladesh’s young population as the country’s greatest potential, he said, “More than one million students pass the Higher Secondary Certificate examinations every year, of whom around 20,000 pursue engineering studies.” However, he noted that engineering education institutions do not all follow the same standards.

Stressing the need for a common framework for accreditation and assessment to ensure educational quality, Mahdi Amin said, “The government wants to bring more engineering degree programmes offered by universities across the country under the accreditation framework.” To achieve this, the Bangladesh Accreditation Council (BAC) and BAETE will coordinate their efforts. He said BAETE could play a role in this process in coordination with the BAC. He also stated that the government would provide policy support to implement the initiative by leveraging the international recognition of the Washington Accord.

At the event, BAC Chairman Professor Md Akhter Hossain Khan said, “Receiving accreditation does not mean the work is complete. It marks the beginning of continuous improvement in educational quality.” He stressed the need to assess whether students acquire the required skills. To achieve this, the government, universities, teachers, industry and professional organisations must work together. He added that the BAC and the IEB could make the accreditation system more effective through experience-sharing and coordination.

BAETE Vice-Chairman Professor Sharmin Reza Chowdhury emphasised the importance of assessing the quality of engineering education before granting accreditation. He said, “Accreditation must be given due consideration in government recruitment, professional registration and licensing.” He added that quality engineering education would improve students’ skills and enhance the standing of the profession.

item.title: Islami, Krishi, and BRAC Bank maintain positions in remittance inflows
item.description:
Islami Bank and Bangladesh Krishi Bank have maintained their first and second positions, respectively, in terms of remittance inflows at the end of the first quarter of the ongoing 2026–27 financial year.

Islami Bank has long held the top spot in receiving remittances, while Krishi Bank has climbed to the second position over the past few years.

Both banks had also finished the previous financial year in first and second place. They have sustained this strong performance through the first quarter of the current fiscal year.

This information emerges from an analysis of Bangladesh Bank’s statistics on inward remittances.

Based on data from the three months spanning July to September, Prothom Alo compiled a list of the top 10 banks facilitating remittance inflows into the country.

The list reveals that private sector BRAC Bank follows Islami Bank and Bangladesh Krishi Bank in third place. State-owned Agrani Bank and private sector Trust Bank hold the fourth and fifth positions, respectively.

Meanwhile, Dutch-Bangla Bank, City Bank, Dhaka Bank, Mutual Trust Bank, and Eastern Bank occupy sixth to tenth places, in that order.

According to Bangladesh Bank data, out of the top 10 remittance-receiving banks in the country, two are state-owned while the remaining eight belong to the private sector. Together, these 10 banks brought in approximately US$5.88 billion in remittances during the first three months of the current fiscal year.

Total inward remittances for the country during this first quarter stood at US$8.59 billion. That means, 68 per cent of the total remittances received during the first three months of the financial year were processed through these 10 banks.

New entrants on the list

Data from Bangladesh Bank indicates that, compared to the previous financial year, two new banks have secured spots in the top 10 list during the first quarter of the current fiscal year. They are Dhaka Bank and Mutual Trust Bank.

With their entry, two banks from the previous financial year's top 10 list have been excluded—namely, state-owned Janata Bank and Pubali Bank.

At the end of the last financial year, Islami Bank also topped the list of the 10 banks bringing the highest volume of remittances into the country.

While Krishi Bank held the second place, BRAC Bank third, Trust Bank fourth, and Agrani Bank fifth spot; sixth to tenth positions were occupied by Janata Bank, City Bank, Dutch-Bangla Bank, Eastern Bank, and Pubali Bank, respectively.

This demonstrates that several banks have shifted positions by the end of the first quarter of the current fiscal year.

Trust Bank, which was in fourth position at the end of the last financial year, now sits in fifth place at the end of the first quarter. Trust Bank and Agrani Bank have effectively swapped places.

Janata Bank, previously in sixth position, has fallen out of the list altogether, allowing Dutch-Bangla Bank to move up from eighth to sixth place. City Bank's position remains unchanged in seventh place, while Eastern Bank has moved down to tenth from ninth place at the end of last year.

At the close of the previous financial year, total remittance inflows into the country stood at US$35.59 billion, with more than two-thirds—or 71 per cent—channelled through the aforementioned 10 banks.

When approached for comment, Ahsan Zaman Chowdhury, Managing Director (MD) and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Trust Bank, told Prothom Alo, “When there is strong demand for dollars in the market, banks are more proactive in gathering remittances from overseas. When demand slackens, that drive decreases somewhat. This is because banks are reluctant to incur the costs associated with bringing in dollars unless there is sufficient demand. This was precisely the case for our bank.”

“Owing to lower demand for dollars during the first three months of the current financial year, we scaled back our focus on remittances, which led to the shift in our position. However, demand for dollars has picked up again this month, and our bank is actively working to bring in foreign remittances. We hope to regain our former position by the end of the year,” he added.

item.title: Identities of 26 Bangladeshis killed or injured in airport attack in Saudi Arabia confirmed
item.description:
Two Bangladeshis were killed and another 24 injured in an attack by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi armed group at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia. The identities of all 26 Bangladeshi victims have been confirmed.

According to sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, the two people killed were Shahed Ahmed and Nasrullah Badarpuri.

Shahed was from Madla village in Shahjahanpur upazila of Bogura. His father’s name was Rafiqul Islam and his mother’s name was Shahera Begum. He worked as a plumber on a project in Jeddah for a Saudi contracting company and held a valid residence permit, known as an iqama. After spending leave in Bangladesh following his brother’s death, he was returning to his workplace in Jeddah via Riyadh.

Nasrullah was from Badarpur village in Nangalkot upazila of Cumilla. His father was Mohammad Ullah and his mother was Jahanara Begum. He had travelled to Saudi Arabia to perform Umrah and was waiting at the airport to travel from Riyadh to Jeddah.

24 Bangladeshis Receiving Treatment in Hospitals

According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, citing the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh, 11 of the 24 injured Bangladeshis were working in Saudi Arabia, while 13 had travelled there on Umrah visas. They are receiving treatment at various hospitals in Riyadh.

The Bangladesh Embassy is in contact with hospital authorities to collect detailed information about the injured and ensure they receive medical care.

King Abdullah Hospital

Three Bangladeshis are receiving treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) of this hospital: Hafez Hasan, Kazi Nurullah and Md Omar Faruk.

Hafez Hasan is from Purba Rasulpur in Kamrangirchar, Dhaka. His father is Ishak and his mother is Kamala Begum. He had travelled to Saudi Arabia on an Umrah visa and was waiting at the airport in Riyadh to travel to Jeddah during a transit stop.

Kazi Nurullah is from Ghatura village in Brahmanbaria Sadar upazila. His father is Kazi Zainal Mia and his mother is Shiuli Begum. He had also travelled to Saudi Arabia on an Umrah visa and was waiting at the airport to travel from Riyadh to Jeddah during transit.

Md Omar Faruk is a Bangladeshi working in Saudi Arabia. He was at the airport to travel from Riyadh to Jeddah for work.

Embassy representatives have met the three men, and their conditions have been reported as stable.

Riyadh National Guard Hospital

Two Bangladeshis are receiving treatment here: Saffat Rahman and Md Daudul Islam. Saffat is unconscious.

Saffat is from Badarpur village in Raninagar upazila of Naogaon. His father is Mokhlesar Rahman and his mother is Rokeya Begum.

Daudul is from Badarpur village in Nangalkot upazila of Cumilla. His father is Md Mohib Ullah and his mother is Rokeya Begum.

Both had travelled to Saudi Arabia on Umrah visas and were waiting at the airport in Riyadh to travel to Jeddah during transit.

2 Bangladeshis killed in Houthi missile attack at Riyadh airport, 4 in ICU

Riyadh Medical Hospital

Two Bangladeshis are receiving treatment at this hospital: Md Saidul Islam Sourav and Abul Mansur Md Riaz Uddin.

Saidul is from the Amligola area of Lalbagh, Dhaka. His father is Md Abdul Hai and his mother is Rahima Begum.

Abul Mansur Md Riaz Uddin is from Janata Housing in Mirpur, Dhaka. His father is Md Abul Fazal and his mother is Tajkera Begum.

Both had travelled to Saudi Arabia on Umrah visas and were waiting at the airport in Riyadh to travel to Jeddah during transit.

Prince Sultan Military Hospital

One Bangladeshi, Md Abdullah, is receiving treatment here. He is from Purba Boxnagar in the Demra area of Dhaka. His father is Md Mokhtar Ahmed and his mother is Fazilatun Nesa. He had travelled to Saudi Arabia on an Umrah visa.

Sulaiman Al Habib Hospital, Takhassusi Branch

Three Bangladeshis are receiving treatment at this hospital: Arman Hossain, Mohammad and Faisal Ahmed Abdul Haque.

Arman is from the Ibrahimnagar area of Kamrangirchar, Dhaka. His father is Mojibul Haque and his mother is Shamsun Nahar. He had travelled to Saudi Arabia on an Umrah visa.

Mohammad and Faisal are Bangladeshis working in Saudi Arabia. Both held iqamas, or residence and work permits.

Kingdom Hospital

One Bangladeshi, Rafiq Mia, is receiving treatment here. He works in Saudi Arabia and holds an iqama.

King Fahad Medical City

Three Bangladeshis are receiving treatment here: Ismail Hossain, Misbah Uddin Hira and Raihanul Islam.

Ismail and Raihanul work in Saudi Arabia. Detailed information about Misbah Uddin Hira was not available.

Five Bangladeshis are receiving treatment at this hospital: Salma Akter, Shahadat Hossain, Moshad Ahmed Saikat, Zahid Ahmed and Sobe Sadeq Md Shahjahan Sarkar.

All five work in Saudi Arabia and hold iqamas.

Aster Sanad Hospital

Two Bangladeshis, Asadul Islam and Jamal, are receiving treatment here. Asadul works in Saudi Arabia.

No further details were available about Md Jamal.

Sulaiman Fakeeh Hospital

One Bangladeshi, Nazma Akter, is reportedly receiving treatment at this hospital. However, no information about her could be confirmed.

Sulaiman Al Habib Hospital, Al Sahafa Branch

Two Bangladeshis, Umair and Abdullah Kamil, are receiving treatment here.

The embassy is continuing its efforts to collect detailed information about the injured and ensure they receive appropriate medical care.

Around 500 Bangladeshi passengers stranded

Disruptions to flight operations following the attack left around 500 Bangladeshi passengers stranded at Riyadh airport. They included passengers who had travelled from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia, people visiting to perform Umrah, and travellers waiting for domestic and international flights to various destinations.

According to ministry sources, the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh, with assistance from airport authorities, Saudi immigration officials and the relevant airlines, arranged accommodation, food and alternative travel for stranded passengers.

According to the embassy, accommodation and meals were arranged at the Marriott and Radisson hotels and a residential hall at Princess Nourah University for around 100 passengers at Terminal 3.

In addition, 67 people who had travelled from Bangladesh to perform Umrah and were wearing ihram garments were transported from Riyadh to Jeddah on special buses.

Around 400 Bangladeshi passengers booked on Saudia Airlines flight SV804 from Riyadh to Dhaka, which was cancelled, are being sent home via King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.

Meanwhile, the embassy helped two Bangladeshi employees of Saudia Airlines travelling from Riyadh to Bahrain reach Bahrain through the land border at Al Khobar.

item.title: 303 children live with mothers in prison, report tells HC
item.description:
The Department of Social Services has recommended placing 303 children living with their incarcerated mothers in prisons across the country with close relatives of their choice or in government-run children’s homes, considering their best interests.
In a report submitted to the High Court, the department said the children were regularly monitored through the Offender Reformation and Rehabilitation Association. They were also provided with essential support, including toys, clothing and baby food.
On June 15, the High Court sought a report from prison authorities detailing the number and ages of children living with their mothers in prisons across the country. However, that report has yet to be submitted.
A High Court bench comprising Justice Khizir Ahmed Choudhury and Justice Md Ziaul Haque issued an order and a rule following a writ petition filed by Supreme Court lawyer Kamrun Nahar Mahmud Deepa.
The rule asked why directives should not be issued to take necessary measures to ensure the safety, welfare, education, proper development and fundamental rights of children living in prisons.
Barrister Kamrun Nahar Mahmud Deepa told Bangla Tribune that the Supreme Court was currently in recess and the final hearing on the writ petition would take place after the holidays.
According to Department of Prisons data, 299 children were living with their mothers in the country’s 74 central and district jails as of April 26, 2024. Of them, 153 were girls, and 146 were boys.
Most of the mothers are accused in drug-related cases. Some are serving prison sentences, while others are awaiting trial.
Division-wise, Dhaka accounted for 100 children living with their mothers in prison, followed by Chittagong with 90, Rajshahi with 25, Rangpur with 25, Khulna with 20, Sylhet with 19, Mymensingh with 13 and Barisal with four.
Kashimpur Central Women’s Jail in Gazipur has the highest number of children living with their mothers, according to the report.
While the Department of Social Services report puts the number at 303, the Department of Prisons recorded 299 children as of April 26, 2024.
Deepa believes the discrepancy will become clearer once the authorities concerned explain the differences in the reporting periods and calculation methods used in the two sets of data.

item.title: President calls for ensuring girls’ safety at home, in society and online
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has called for ensuring the safety of girls at home, in schools, in society and online, stressing the need for a zero-tolerance policy and speedy trials in cases of violence against women and children, rape and sexual harassment.
He made the remarks at a programme marking International and National Girl Child Day 2026 at the Bangladesh Shishu Academy auditorium on Monday.
The president said political commitment, administrative efficiency, social participation and, above all, a change in mindset were essential to empowering girls to achieve their full potential.
To prevent child marriage, the government is prioritising poverty alleviation, free education, stipends and stronger social safety nets, alongside verification of birth registrations and expanded opportunities for girls to pursue higher education, he said.
Referring to the killing of Tajmin, the president said: “We are moving forward, yet in some areas, we are regressing. It is the responsibility of guardians to look after their children. The girl from Cumilla was missing from home for three days, yet no concern was evident among her guardians.”
On public safety, he said: “When mothers sit on spread-out newspapers near schools waiting to take their children home, it reveals just how unsafe society has become.”
