item.title: Bangladesh seeks stronger energy ties with Saudi Arabia, Qatar
item.description:
Bangladesh has sought stronger energy cooperation with Saudi Arabia and Qatar while exploring foreign investment opportunities in its renewable energy sector during a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the 17th International Energy Forum held in Riyadh.
State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit held separate meetings with Saudi Assistant Minister of Energy for Electricity Nasser bin Hadi Al-Qahtani, Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs and Qatar Energy President and CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, and ACWA Power CEO Dr Samir J Serhan, according to a message received on Monday.
The discussions focused on strengthening Bangladesh's energy security, securing long-term liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies, expanding bilateral cooperation and attracting foreign investment in renewable energy.
During his meeting with Saudi Assistant Minister Nasser Al-Qahtani, Amit expressed condolences over the deaths caused by a Houthi rebel attack at Riyadh International Airport and condemned the attack. He reaffirmed the solidarity of the government and people of Bangladesh with Saudi Arabia and briefed the Saudi official on the condolence message sent by Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to the Saudi crown prince and prime minister.
The Bangladesh state minister also sought Saudi Arabia's assistance in repatriating the bodies of two Bangladeshi nationals killed in the attack and ensuring medical treatment for those injured.
On energy cooperation, Amit sought Saudi support to strengthen Bangladesh's energy security. In response, the Saudi official described Bangladesh as a brotherly country that holds special importance for the Saudi government and expressed optimism about further expanding ongoing cooperation in energy security and other development initiatives.
The two sides stressed exchanging delegations and establishing a framework for understanding to discuss areas of Saudi support for Bangladesh's efforts to achieve its energy targets by 2030.
The discussions also covered long-term energy cooperation, the development of floating LNG terminals, and offshore and onshore gas exploration.
In his meeting with Qatar's State Minister for Energy Affairs Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Amit discussed Bangladesh's growing demand for natural gas, its existing LNG import arrangements and the possibility of signing new long-term supply agreements.
The two sides also explored LNG supplies from Qatar Energy's international portfolio and the diversification of supply sources and routes to strengthen Bangladesh's energy security. Both ministers stressed the need for continuing commercial and technical discussions between the relevant organisations.
In a third meeting, ACWA Power CEO Dr Samir J Serhan discussed investment opportunities in Bangladesh's renewable energy sector with the state minister. ACWA Power expressed interest in investing in the country's renewable energy sector.
Officials from the Bangladesh delegation and the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh were present at the meetings.

item.title: War and peace
item.description:
On the evening of February 24, 2022, I was due to teach an internal medicine session to a group of junior colleagues, among them a young physician from Ukraine.
She could not speak through her tears, and could not attend. Russian tanks had crossed her country's border hours earlier. I remember the silence on that call more clearly than almost anything said in it.
On the morning of October 7, 2023, I woke early and watched, in something close to real time, young people being dragged away from a music festival in southern Israel, and the destruction, within hours, of the Israeli villages bordering Gaza. Within perhaps half a day, hundreds were dead.
In the months since October 7, 2023, I have watched, night after night, as Gaza was reduced to rubble, hospitals bombed to ashes, and aid workers killed while children ran toward soup kitchens holding out bent and broken utensils, while white-painted drones circled overhead and IDF mortars piercing the sky above the blue Mediterranean.
And this year, a third conflict opened before I had recovered from the second: Iran and the United States, missiles fired across the Gulf, Saudi Arabia itself struck by Iranian fire meant for someone else.
Three theatres. Three of the most technologically advanced militaries in human history, deploying precision munitions, autonomous drones, and missile-defense systems worth billions of dollars.
And the result, in every case, is not zero. It is sub-zero.
More dead than before the shooting started. No peace concluded. No side visibly deterred.
Gaza in ruins. Ukraine still waiting for an end no one can date. The Gulf still bracing for the war's next act.
I have carried this fear since I was young enough to watch the towers fall in New York in 2001 -- nearly live, on the BBC, in the hospital corridor where I was on duty.
A nurse burst through the door, breathless, calling out my name twice -- “Rajani! Rajani!” -- as though the news itself could not wait for a full sentence. Some planes, she said, had struck the roof of a tower in New York.
Even Swedish radio, usually so measured, could not yet decipher what was happening, and for a long moment neither could we, standing together in that corridor, disbelieving.
And the tragic aftermath of nearly two decades of war that followed -- in Iraq, Syria, and Afghanistan -- still haunts a generation of women denied their schooling, wrapped head to foot in black, in Kabul and elsewhere, in what was once a more modern country.
Weeks, months later, came a similar news alert: Netanyahu had ordered civilians in southern Lebanon to flee before a bombing spree. That same evening, sharing this over dinner with a friend, I found myself asking aloud what would happen if Putin attacked Sweden and told us to flee.
Flee where? For one unsettling moment, I did not want to know whether I was Lebanese, or Swedish, or a Bengali. I was simply a disposable object, waiting to be thrown into the trash of human folly.
And where does the Iran-US war fit into this -- a war still ongoing, its fragile ceasefires broken. I think here of a friend's son, married to an Iranian physician. On at least two occasions, she has flown to Sweden from elsewhere in the EU -- and each time, within days, as though summoned by some cruel and uncanny clock, a new round of bombing has broken out between the US and Iran.
I have joked with her, half-seriously by now: Whenever you are in Sweden, the US bombs Iran. But behind the joke sits something that is not funny at all -- her parents, still in Tehran, waiting out each night not knowing whether the next siren is the one that finally reaches them. Safe, so far. Only so far.
High technology has changed how efficiently human beings can kill one another. It has not changed why we do it, and it has not once, in any of these three wars, produced the thing weapons are supposedly for: Peace.
On August 7, 2026, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement in the city for which it is named -- a pact declaring that an armed attack on any one signatory will be treated as an attack on all three.
Commentators have already nicknamed it a “Sunni NATO,” though it has none of NATO's command structure, and its own foreign ministers insist it targets no one.
It was born, transparently, from the last 18 months: Saudi Arabia absorbing Iranian missile fire, Gulf states losing confidence that Washington will backstop their security in real time.
What concerns me is not the pact itself -- sovereign nations may organize their own defense as they judge wisest.
What concerns me is what comes next. Bangladeshi officials have confirmed that Saudi Arabia has invited Dhaka to consider joining. A junior foreign minister has called the idea something Bangladesh “views positively.” Nothing is decided. But the invitation is real, and so is the danger it opens.
Bangladesh has no quarrel with Iran. It has no stake in the Gulf. But under a mutual-defense clause, an attack on any member becomes everyone's war -- and Bangladesh's two nearest neighbours are nuclear-armed and have fought each other four times since 1947. The Radcliffe Line still runs raw through this region's memory.
Let me say plainly what I am not saying, because in this country, a byline is often read before an argument is. My surname will be filed by some readers, reflexively, as Hindu, and from there as pro-Indian -- a conflation as old and as unjust as the Radcliffe Line itself.
I write none of this out of sympathy for India over Pakistan, or Pakistan over India. I do not want Bangladesh dragged into a war against India, and I do not want it dragged into a war against Iran on Saudi Arabia's behalf, for exactly the same reason: I am against every war, everywhere, without exception, and I do not believe any Bangladeshi, of any faith, gains anything from a grave.
I say this as someone whose mother still lives in Dhaka, and who has, by his own choice, become something other than only Bangladeshi. Sweden is my home now.
I have watched Gaza's children, Tehran's children, and Ukraine's children -- and a Ukrainian doctor unable to speak through her tears -- with the same grief, because I claim no side except the side of those who did not choose any of it.
If Bangladesh is pulled into a war between India and Pakistan or over a Gulf dispute it never chose, the only outcome will be death -- Bangladeshi death, achieving nothing for Bangladesh.
There is a class of victims in these wars that rarely makes the front page, and I have not been able to stop thinking about them.
When the fighting between Iran and the United States widened into the Gulf this year, I watched footage of a drone strike setting fire to fuel tanks near Dubai International Airport -- an airport I have passed through so many times on my way to Dhaka or elsewhere that I could not, at first, quite believe what I was seeing.
What frightened me most, though, was not the airport. It was the millions of people from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and India who live and work across the Gulf states -- the drivers, nurses, construction workers, and domestic staff whose labour keeps those economies running, and whose remittances keep millions of families afloat back home.
Human rights organizations have already confirmed that Bangladeshi, Pakistani, and Nepali workers were killed in strikes on Gulf cities during this war -- a driver, a security guard, a water-tanker operator, ordinary people who chose this war no more than the residents of Gaza or Kharkiv did. In fact, two Bangladeshis were killed in the recent attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on October 10.
Had the fighting widened rather than paused, the danger to those workers would not have been only physical. It would also have been the danger of unemployment overnight -- a war turning millions of already vulnerable labourers into returnees with no income and no plan, in economies that cannot easily absorb them.
That fear sat in me with exactly the same weight as watching Gaza's children run toward a soup kitchen. A migrant worker killed in Dubai and a starving child in Gaza are not different categories of grief. They are the same failure, wearing different clothes.
Even the world's richest and most powerful nation cannot make the arithmetic of modern weaponry work.
A single Patriot interceptor takes years to build. The United States, still the strongest military and economic power on Earth, is nonetheless carrying a national debt now near forty trillion dollars, growing by billions of dollars every single day.
If a country of that wealth and scale cannot spend its way to peace through weapons, what should a country like Bangladesh conclude?
And this is not a hypothetical question for Bangladesh. Dhaka has recently advanced a deal to buy up to two dozen Chinese J-10CE fighter jets, at a cost reported near $2bn -- one of the largest defense procurements in the country's history.
Reasonable people can debate whether Bangladesh needs to modernize its air force. Probably it does. But before any such sum is committed, its politicians owe the public more than a single moment's reflection. They owe it a dozen.
What could two billion dollars buy in hospitals, schools, flood defenses, for a country that still struggles to fund all three?
Every taka spent on a fighter jet is a taka that cannot feed a child, treat a patient, or build a seawall against the rising water that will, with rising certainty, arrive before any invading army does.
This is the part of the ledger the war planners never show. Every high-tech weapon is a bet that violence, or the credible threat of it, will purchase something -- territory, deterrence, security, victory.
Three live wars, watched in real time by the whole world, have now tested that bet at unprecedented scale and technological sophistication. In every case, the bet has lost. Not broken even. Lost. No child's death has ever repaired a balance sheet. No missile fired has ever paid down a debt.
I write none of this from resentment toward the United States. I say this as a physician whose own career would not exist in its present form without America -- its conferences, its training programs, its medical journals and universities, the sheer excellence of its scientific culture.
I admire it, unreservedly, and I want it strong. That is exactly why watching its finances stretched thin by war, and its own missile stockpiles too depleted to properly defend an ally, causes me grief rather than any satisfaction.
A country I admire should not have to choose between its own future and one more interceptor.
I once spent six months working in Riyadh, and I still remember flying in and out of that city, looking down at a skyline that had not existed within living memory, and wondering, honestly, how it had been built.
Decades earlier, as a PhD student, I had discussed something similar with younger Swedish colleagues -- what people then called the postwar Western miracle: How ruined economies had rebuilt themselves not through conquest but through trade, institutions, and the free movement of people, capital, and ideas.
What I saw from the air over Riyadh, and later over Doha and Dubai, struck me as a second version of the same miracle: Glass towers and universities and airports risen from the desert within two generations, built by planning and investment rather than war.
Whatever one thinks of how that wealth arrived, its existence is a genuine human achievement -- proof that peace, prosperity, human mobility, and the free flow of capital and information are what progress actually looks like, in the Gulf as much as in the West.
None of it was built by weapons. All of it is now, in different ways, being asked to live under weapons' shadow.
That is the deeper waste: Not merely the money spent on armaments, but the fact that it is being subtracted from precisely the kinds of projects -- scientific, medical, economic, civic -- that have actually made nations great.
As a physician, I cannot stop thinking of it in those terms: Every fighter jet and every interceptor is money that did not go toward cancer research, or the next Ebola outbreak, or the next pandemic we have not yet named.
We know, because we have watched it happen twice in this decade already, that we are not owed advance warning.
If there is a lesson buried in seventy years of failed deterrence, it is not military. It is political.
The only durable peace project of the modern era is the European Union -- a continent that fought itself to exhaustion twice in 30 years, and has not fought itself once since 1945.
As a result, a Dane can breakfast in Copenhagen, lunch in Vienna, and dine in Paris, crossing what used to be the most contested borders on Earth without a checkpoint in sight today.
No missile shield built that. Shared institutions did -- habits of coexistence, patiently assembled, chosen over and over rather than imposed once.
South Asia has never had its Schuman moment -- the 1950 declaration that first bound France’s and Germany’s coal and steel industries together and became the seed from which the European Union grew.
It should not need a war to go looking for one. But it could still choose, deliberately, to become the region that tried.
Rajani K Saha writes from Sweden and is a practising physician.

item.title: Clean air is not a luxury
item.description:
Dhaka woke up on Sunday to an Air Quality Index reading of 167, which the index classifies as "unhealthy."
Dhaka has long been among the most polluted cities in the world, and yet, with winter fast approaching and the imminent threat of air that is simply not fit to breathe, we continue to do little to address it.
The causes are no mystery: Brick kilns on the city's fringes, many operating with little regard for the rules; construction sites that leave sand and debris uncovered; roads dug up and rebuilt in a never-ending cycle; and a clogged, fume-spewing traffic system.
What remains missing is the will to act on them. Every year, the authorities announce drives, fines, and demolitions, and every year, the air gets no cleaner. Such efforts begin loudly, fade quietly, and return only when the numbers make headlines again.
Pollution control cannot be a seasonal activity, any more than breathing is.
The cost, meanwhile, is being paid by ordinary people. The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution kills around seven million people worldwide each year, mostly through stroke, heart disease, lung cancer, and respiratory infections.
For those in Dhaka, where millions are outdoors at all times, those figures show up in crowded hospital corridors, missed school days, and lost income.
By now, there are no secrets to solutions: From construction sites needing to follow dust control rules, to brick kilns needing to be regulated, to accelerating cleaner energy and technologies that already exist.
Clean air should never be viewed as a luxury nor a favour. It is something every citizen is owed. A city that cannot guarantee it has failed at the most basic test of governance.
We should not wait for the smog to thicken before we remember that. The time to act is now, while we can still breathe.

item.title: Fixing our banking sector
item.description:
Reports that the International Monetary Fund will likely press for strict, time-bound deadlines to fix weak banks and reduce the astronomical non-performing loans (NPLs) we have racked up should serve as a wake-up call for our leaders.
Despite dreams of self-sufficiency, the reality we must contend with is that, at present, our economic delegations are preparing to negotiate a fresh financial package with international lenders.
To that end, it is also abundantly clear that if we are to continue to receive the financial assistance our economy needs, Bangladesh can no longer afford half-measures in reforming what can safely be referred to as its crippled banking sector.
Decades of political patronage, reckless default cultures, and opaque loan write-offs have brought our financial architecture to the brink. As such, we simply no longer have the option to treat bank reform as an optional administrative exercise.
The rot in our financial system is neither hidden nor new. For years, massive amounts of liquidity have been siphoned off through fraud, insider lending, and willful defaults, leaving state-owned and private commercial banks saddled with staggering piles of debt.
It goes without saying that a banking sector choking on defaulted loans cannot be of help to the economy, thereby stunting our growth and deepening the broader fiscal crisis.
While no nation likes external pressure, we would do well to not view it as an infringement on sovereignty, but rather as a catalyst for accountability.
Financial stability is the backbone of national security and economic survival, and it is a shame that Bangladesh has not experienced it for some time now, if ever.
If setting strict deadlines is what is needed to cleanse our balance sheets and end the culture of loan default, then so be it. We must do what we can to restore public trust and build a modern, transparent banking system.

item.title: Greener Garments Initiative, Jamuna Group sign agreement for 34 MWp rooftop solar
item.description:
Greener Garments Initiative (GGI) has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Jamuna Group to install 34 MWp of solar panels on the rooftops of Jamuna Group’s factories.
It is the largest operating expense (Opex) rooftop solar agreement in the commercial and industrial sector of its kind in Bangladesh to date.
The Opex agreement was signed on Thursday, October 8, at the Bestseller office in Gulshan, Dhaka.
Sumaiya Rozalin Islam, group director of Jamuna Group, and Nure Alam, chief executive officer of GGI, signed on behalf of their organizations.
GGI board chairman Willem Grimminck and GGI board director Sebastian Groh were also present at the event.
Also present from Jamuna Group were Engr AKM Kamal, senior general manager, utility; Saiful Islam, head of legal; and Golam Sorwar Mozomder, senior general manager, accounts and finance.
From GGI and SOLshare, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, chief technology officer, and Aziza Sultana Mukti, deputy CEO, also attended.
GGI will fully finance the rooftop solar plants. Its founding partner, SOLshare, will engineer, procure, and commission (EPC) them, then operate and maintain them for the next 20 years.
Jamuna Group will make no upfront investment and will pay for the electricity the systems produce.
Once running, the systems are expected to generate 46,000 MWh of clean electricity while cutting about 30,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions per year, roughly the amount absorbed by more than one million trees in a year.
Jamuna Group’s factories also produce for Bestseller, the global family-owned fashion company.
Running these factories on solar power supports Bestseller’s Scope 3 emission reductions, which are the emissions from its supply chain, and helps it source greener fashion.
“For manufacturers in Bangladesh, rooftop solar is a business decision. It helps factories meet EU requirements, strengthens their relationships with customers, lowers energy costs and gives them the power they need to keep production lines running,” commented Willem Grimminck, chairman of the board, GGI.
“With this partnership, our factories will run on cleaner power. Jamuna Group is committed to cutting carbon emissions and meeting the compliance standards of our buyers. This model supports us in doing both, and helps us stay competitive as an exporter”, said Sumaiya Rozalin Islam, group director of Jamuna Group.
“Solar is where we start, but GGI offers a range of decarbonization solutions for factories, including battery storage, heat recovery, energy efficiency and water treatment. We take care of the cleaner energy and decarbonization side, so manufacturers can cut emissions across their whole operation and stay focused on their core business. We are ready to work with more factories in Bangladesh that want to make the same move,” added Nure Alam, CEO of GGI.

item.description:

item.title: JU student goes missing; ‘suicide note’ found in hall room
item.description:
Md Mohaiminul Islam, a student of the 50th batch of the Department of Geological Sciences at Jahangirnagar University (JU), has gone missing.
Mohaiminul, from Hazra Bari in Melandah upazila of Jamalpur, was last seen boarding a bus in front of his dormitory at 3:08pm on Sunday, according to university administration sources.
He is a resident student of Room 110 in Block A of the hall. Despite attempts to contact him, his whereabouts remain unknown.
A general diary was filed at Savar police station, and Dhaka District Superintendent of Police Shamima Parvin was informed of the incident.
In a separate notice, the university’s Public Relations Office said a “suicide note” had been found in the student’s room. As the note reportedly mentions negligence by the department, the JU administration has formed an investigation committee.
Professor Dr Muhammad Nazrul Islam, the university’s pro-vice-chancellor (administration), said the university administration, proctorial body and police were working to locate the student. They were also contacting his friends, relatives and acquaintances.
The university authorities have urged anyone with information about Mohaiminul’s whereabouts to contact the proctor at 01714012315 or the security officer at 01712674557.

item.title: Litton ton powers Bangladesh to set Afghanistan 479-run target
item.description:
Bangladesh wicketkeeper-batter Litton Das struck a superb century as the Tigers built a massive target for Afghanistan in the one-off Test at Sheikh Zayed Stadium in Abu Dhabi on Monday.
Litton's hundred strengthened Bangladesh's position in the match after the visitors established a 106-run first-innings lead, thanks largely to a devastating bowling display from Hasan Mahmud and Ebadot Hossain on the third day.
Bangladesh had finished Sunday's play at 223-6 in their second innings, extending their overall lead to 329 runs. Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto scored 82 and veteran batter Mushfiqur Rahim made 81 to rescue the innings after the Tigers slipped to 53-3.
Litton, who resumed the fourth morning unbeaten on five, capitalised on two dropped catches to reach his century and put Bangladesh firmly in control. His partnership with Mehidy Hasan Miraz proved crucial in frustrating Afghanistan's bowlers and extending the visitors' advantage.
Mehidy also made a valuable contribution, supporting Litton as Bangladesh's seventh-wicket stand carried the total beyond 300. The pair's resistance ensured Afghanistan faced a daunting challenge in the fourth innings.
Earlier, Afghanistan were dismissed for 240 in reply to Bangladesh's first-innings 346. Hasan Mahmud claimed 5-55, including a hat-trick, becoming the first Bangladesh fast bowler to achieve the feat in Test cricket. Ebadot Hossain complemented him with four wickets.
Afghanistan captain Rahmat Shah had earlier scored an unbeaten 105, while Abdul Malik contributed 62, but their efforts could not prevent Bangladesh from securing a significant first-innings deficit.
Bangladesh eventually declared their second innings at 372-7, setting Afghanistan a target of 479 runs for victory.
The Tigers will now look to their bowlers to finish the job and secure a memorable Test victory.

item.title: 'Amazing feeling': Hasan reflects on historic Test hat-trick
item.description:
Bangladesh quick Hasan Mahmud has admitted it was a surreal feeling when he became the first fast bowler from his country to complete a Test hat-trick.
Mahmud completed the feat in the one-off Test against Afghanistan in Abu Dhabi when he ripped through the opposition's batting lineup on his way to collecting another five-wicket haul.
The right-armer becomes just the third player from Bangladesh to register a hat-trick in a Test match and the first fast bowler to do so, joining Alok Kapali (v Pakistan in 2003) and Sohag Gazi (v New Zealand in 2013) as the only players from the country to register three consecutive dismissals in a Test.
Mahmud first deceived Ismat Alam to uproot his off-stump, before he removed Qais Ahmad and Zia-ur-Rehman with consecutive deliveries to clinch the rare hat-trick.
“It's an amazing feeling," Mahmud said at stumps on day three of the Test after Bangladesh reached 223/6 in their second innings to lead by 329 runs overall.
"When you start bowling and see movement off the wicket, you try to bowl upright, swing the ball and get a wicket.
"I was just trying that and following my process. I was pleased to see this kind of movement in the morning."
It helped continue a rich vein of form for Mahmud, who in August led Bangladesh to a memorable Test triumph over Australia in Darwin with a nine-wicket match haul as the side continued their push up the ICC World Test Championship standings.
This fixture against Afghanistan isn't part of the World Test Championship cycle, but Mahmud's form was just as impressive as the seamer collected four wickets overall on the third day to finish with figures of 5/55 from 21 economical overs.
Mahmud paid credit to Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto and experienced batter Litton Das for playing their part in the hat-trick, after the duo convinced him to review the decisive LBW decision against Zia-ur-Rehman to ensure he completed the feat.
“Last day I only got one wicket the whole day, but I wasn't nervous at all. I was looking forward to today,” Mahmud said.
“We lost a couple of DRS in the first innings, so everyone was thinking about the DRS, whether it was going to be hitting or not. Credit to the captain and Litton Das. They were talking and chatting with each other, and then they told me that it was going to hit, so I could take the review.
“I just felt that I should bowl straight. That's it. Let the ball do the job. So I just followed the line and bowled at the top of the stumps."

item.title: Isco nets brace as Betis rise back above Real Madrid to third
item.description:
Veteran playmaker Isco struck twice to help Real Betis climb back into third place in La Liga with a 5-2 win over Osasuna on Sunday.
The Andalucian side moved a point above Real Madrid, fourth, and level with second place Atletico Madrid, trailing leaders Barca by five points.
Manuel Pellegrini's side claimed a sixth league win from eight matches with an exciting display of attacking football at La Cartuja stadium, where they are playing until their Benito Villamarin home is renovated, likely 2028.
Former Real Madrid midfielder Isco, 34, netted from the penalty spot after a foul on Rodrigo Riquelme, and Ez Abde doubled the hosts lead after half-an-hour with a cool finish.
Ante Budimir's own goal gave Betis their third after half-time, before the Croatian striker netted at the correct and Raul Garcia added another to give Osasuna a fighting chance.
Isco capitalised on a loose ball in the box to grab his second and Jose Morante bagged a fifth in stoppage time to close out Betis's big win.
"Football is never truly under control," said Pellegrini after his side almost let their three-goal lead slip.
"As soon as the pace drops, the other team can pull level."
The former Manchester City coach also praised Isco after his brace.
"He has spectacular quality and a maturity as a player that allows him to perform at whatever level he wants to," added Pellegrini.
Elsewhere Valencia, 19th, earned a point in a 2-2 draw at Racing Santander under new coach Javier Aguirre.
Real Sociedad defeated Deportivo La Coruna 3-2 in another entertaining battle.
The Basque side, sixth, eased into a three-goal lead Mario Soriano pulled one back for the visitors in San Sebastian to spark a Depor fight back.
They were given further encouragement when Real Sociedad's Pablo Marin was sent off in the 66th minute for a foul on Nsongo Bil in the box and Yeremay Hernandez netted from the penalty spot.
Both teams finished with 10 men after Lorenzo Amatucci brought down Mikel Oyarzabal as the last man, and Depor could not find an equaliser.
On Saturday Liga leaders Barcelona beat Getafe 3-0 to prolong their perfect start to the season, with eight wins from eight league games.
Hansi Flick's side are followed by second place Atletico Madrid, who snatched a late 2-1 win at Alaves, while Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid scraped a 1-0 victory over Villarreal despite Vinicius Junior's red card for hair-pulling.

item.title: City shrug off uncertain future to beat 10-man Liverpool
item.description:
Manchester City shrugged off the threat of swingeing sanctions to beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in their first game since being found guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules.
Second-half goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki extended City's flawless start under Enzo Maresca after Ryan Gravenberch had been sent off for two yellow cards.
City re-established their three-point lead at the top of the table, but the future of any title challenge rests on the outcome of the club's appeal against widespread financial impropriety.
"We need to learn how to deal with the outside noise, but make our own noise, which is to win games," said Maresca.
"Our fans were singing at the end, so the noise was from us."
An independent commission found City and their Emirati owners arranged "sham" deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018.
No sanction has yet been handed down, but a severe points deduction or even expulsion from the English top flight are on the table unless City overturn the decision.
There has even been speculation there could be retrospective action to strip titles.
"The uncertainty is not good for anyone," said Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola.
The multiple breaches of Premier League laws came during a period in which City won three titles and a clutch of other trophies.
City's rivals believe, however, that the illegal spending during that period also built the foundations for a golden era under former boss Pep Guardiola, who left at the end of last season.
Liverpool were one of the clubs most affected, having finished second to City three times in the past 12 years.
"City have fundamentally cheated to win those leagues," Jamie Gallaghie, a 48-year-old teacher, told AFP.
The visitors arrived under the protection of a police escort with a hostile Anfield welcome expected, but there was no repeat of the violent scenes when their team bus was pelted by bottles ahead of a Champions League clash in 2018.
Liverpool fans lined the streets to greet the City players with chants of "cheats" and "going down", while merchandise stalls were littered with flags and scarves mocking their rivals' financial scandal.
In the iconic Kop end behind one goal a banner read "a generation of supporters cheated."
The battles between Guardiola's City and Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool in recent years became the Premier League's marquee event.
But with the eyes of the world watching, Liverpool failed to rise to the occasion on the field.
New Liverpool boss Iraola's options were blunted without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo as the Spaniard suffered his first defeat since taking charge of the Reds.
An Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008 transformed City from mid-table mediocrity into the dominant force of the English game.
City's economic might was on full show and helped turn the game as Maresca could introduce Doku off the bench early in the second half.
Within minutes the Belgian winger had been chopped down by Gravenberch, who was shown a harsh second booking, and Liverpool never recovered.
Doku's deflected shot was then smashed home by Haaland to break the deadlock 25 minutes from time, opening the floodgates.
Three minutes later Doku curled a sensational strike into the top corner himself.
Cherki then exchanged a slick one-two with Josko Gvardiol before slotting under Alisson Becker to rub salt in Liverpool wounds.
The defeat leaves Liverpool nine points adrift of the leaders down in ninth.

item.title: Abhishek, Arshdeep shine in India's Indore triumph
item.description:
A run-filled contest took over in Indore as a collective 432 runs were scored across 40 overs, with India ultimately emerging victors by 14 runs and going ahead 2-1 in the five-match T20I series.
Opener Abhishek Sharma top-scored for India with a quickfire 69 as the hosts amassed a good total of 223 and a disciplined bowling performance ensured the West Indies were held to just 209/7 in reply.
Left-armer Arshdeep Singh (3/44) was the pick of the bowlers and was adjudged Player of the Match for his efforts, but India skipper Shreyas Iyer was impressed with the performance from his entire bowling group.
"It was wonderful to see the bowlers being confident," Iyer said post-match.
"The clarity was very much visible when I was interacting. They were ready to take up the challenge and that's what we want."
West Indies captain Shai Hope was left to lament a couple of telling mistakes with the ball that allowed India to post such a competitive total.
"Probably with the ball, we could've executed a little bit better," Hope said.
"So those little margins would be the deciding factor come the end of the game."
India were put in to bat first and after Sanju Samson fell for just three runs, Abhishek took charge of the innings with a blistering 69 off 30 deliveries, which included six fours and five sixes.
Ishan Kishan continued the assault, scoring a quickfire 37 off 18 balls as India raced to 115 in just 8.2 overs. Roston Chase brought Kishan's innings to an end to provide the West Indies with a timely breakthrough.
Tilak Varma added further impetus with a brisk 28 off 16 deliveries before a bizarre run-out cut short his stay at the crease.
India maintained their aggressive approach in the latter stages, with Nitish Kumar Reddy (21 off 14) and Axar Patel (20 off 14) chipping in with valuable contributions to keep the scoreboard moving.
Prince Yadav then provided a late flourish, striking three boundaries in the final over as India were bowled out for 223.
Chase (2/38), Shamar Springer (2/54) and Shamar Joseph (2/54) claimed two wickets apiece for the visitors.
In reply, the West Indies endured a disastrous start as Hope, who had struck a century in the second T20I, was cleaned up by Arshdeep for five in the second over.
Shimron Hetmyer and Kamil Pooran then launched a spirited counterattack, putting together a 60-run partnership for the second wicket off just 31 deliveries.
Hetmyer smashed 43 off 26 balls, while Pooran contributed 42 off 27, briefly shifting the momentum in the visitors' favour.
Naman Dhir, however, struck at a crucial juncture to dismiss both set batters and swing the contest back in India's favour.
Sherfane Rutherford (32 off 20) and Quentin Sampson (21 off 15) attempted to revive the chase, but India continued to chip away at the wickets and prevented the West Indies from building another substantial partnership.
Springer brought out some surprise fireworks at the end with a breathtaking 35* from just 11 balls, but India ultimately sealed the deal by 14 runs.
Arshdeep led the bowling effort with figures of 3/44, receiving valuable support from Naman Dhir (2/39), Axar Patel (1/33) and Nitish Kumar Reddy (1-19).
The fourth T20I will take place in Hyderabad on Wednesday, 14 October.

item.title: Sadaqat, Imran help Pakistan thump Sri Lanka to seal T20 series
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat just missed out on a hundred as Pakistan upstaged Sri Lanka by 82 runs in the second T20 international on Sunday, taking an unbeatable 2-0 lead in the series.
Sadaqat's 51-ball 96 and Sahibzada Farhan's 44-ball 73 helped Pakistan to their highest T20 total at home of 215-3 in Rawalpindi.
Medium pacer Mohammad Imran then grabbed 3-11 to restrict Sri Lanka to 133-7 for Pakistan's biggest T20 win over the tourists.
Sri Lanka lost wickets at regular intervals with Maheesh Theekshana (32 not out) and Chamindu Wickramasinghe (29) offering some resistance once the game was beyond reach.
Kamindu Mendis (23) and Sineth Jayawardena (22) were the only others to reach double figures.
Pakistan benefited from three dropped catches by Sri Lanka as Sadaqat and Farhan punished the attack, adding 88 runs for the second wicket off just 49 balls.
Sadaqat smashed seven sixes -- the joint most by a Pakistan batter in a T20s -- and six fours before being dismissed off the final delivery of the innings.
Farhan, dropped on two and 11, hit five sixes and four fours before he holed out to Dasun Shanaka in the 15th over.
Sadaqat, who was put down on 44, then cut loose and added a quickfire 72 off 31 balls for the third wicket with Hasan Nawaz (19 not out).
Pakistan plundered 70 runs in the last five overs, improving on their highest home T20 total of 208-3 against the West Indies in Karachi five years ago.
The third and final match is on Tuesday.

item.title: France’s high school students plan fresh protests
item.description:
France’s high school students on Monday begin a new stage of their campaign for improved conditions, hoping to maintain the momentum with a fresh wave of demonstrations.
The new protests, scheduled for Tuesday, could be a turning point in the movement, launched in mid-September, which the government hopes is already winding down.
On Friday, the government noted a dramatic drop in the number of blockades and meetings outside the country’s lycees, where students -- most between 15 and 18 -- complete their high school education.
More than 96% were opening Friday, said the education ministry.
The authorities are all the more keen to see the student protests end given that online activists have called for demonstrations next Saturday to protest the cost of living.
For President Emmanuel Macron’s administration, that brings back troubling memories of the grassroots Yellow Vest movement.
Their protests, launched in 2018 over a planned fuel tax rise, saw massive demonstrations and clashes between police and protesters that shook the presidency during Macron’s first term in office.
The government is still counting the cost of the high school protests.
A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations was “at least 30 million euros.”
On Friday, the justice ministry said more than 6,800 people had been detained since the demonstrations started, 86 percent of them minors.
After clashes between some protesters and riot police left some students severely injured, sparking criticism of police tactics, the government suspended the use of stun grenades that cost one student his hand.
Police are investigating 18 alleged cases of misconduct within their ranks.
Last week, the government came up with concrete proposals to try to address the students’ demands.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced late Thursday that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Sunday promised to make changes to the planned budget 2027 to respond to some demands set out in an online platform the government set up to gather students’ views.
The student organizations behind the protests are yet to be convinced, however.
The Union of High School students described the initial announcements last week as “crumbs.” They are maintaining their demand for an extra 10 million euros to be invested in the country’s lycees.
France’s 10,000 medical students, however, are beginning to express concern at the effect any continued school blockades could have on exams starting Monday that help determine their eventual speciality.
They do not want to see the students’ action disrupt such a crucial stage of their education.
Last Thursday’s student demonstrations mobilized tens of thousands of people across France: 71,500 according to interior ministry figures.
Nearly 256,000 took part in last Tuesday’s day of action.
And one poll, carried out by Ipsos-BVA and published on Sunday, said 54% of respondents backed the high school student protests.
They had the most sympathy with student complaints about the excessive size of classes and with the need to renovate the country’s crumbling schools.

item.title: Flights grounded, livelihoods at risk
item.description:
At least 5,418 passengers travelling from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia have been affected by disruptions to 51 flights following the deadly attack on Riyadh’s international airport, leaving hundreds of expatriate workers facing uncertainty over their jobs, visas and return to the kingdom.
The crisis deepened on Monday as the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) confirmed the cancellation of 12 Dhaka-Riyadh flights over three days, while the government announced plans to arrange alternative travel through Medina and Dammam for workers whose visas are nearing expiry.
The disruptions have affected both direct and connecting flights, with passengers stranded at Dhaka’s Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and others forced to return home without knowing when they can travel.
Many are migrant workers returning to Saudi Arabia after visiting their families. For them, the uncertainty extends beyond cancelled flights to the possibility of losing their livelihoods.
The aviation disruption follows Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which killed two Bangladeshis and injured 24 others, according to Bangladesh’s foreign ministry.
According to CAAB data, 51 flights connecting Bangladesh with Saudi Arabia have been affected by the suspension of operations at Saudi airports.
Of these, 12 are direct flights and 39 involve transit connections. Some have been cancelled, while others remain suspended or disrupted.
As of Monday afternoon, CAAB confirmed that 12 Riyadh-bound flights from Dhaka had been cancelled since Saturday.
These include four operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, two by US-Bangla Airlines, three by Saudia and three by Riyadh Air.
The cancelled flights were scheduled to carry 4,815 passengers, according to the authority.
CAAB Assistant Director (Public Relations) Muhammad Kawsar Mahmud told Dhaka Tribune that the cancellations had caused serious inconvenience to more than 4,000 passengers.
He said airlines would announce revised schedules after assessing the situation.
“We have advised passengers to stay in touch with the airlines,” he added.
Reuters reported that flight operations at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport had been suspended following the attack.
Airport authorities advised travellers to confirm their flight status with airlines before travelling to the airport.
Flight-tracking information from Flightradar24 also indicated widespread cancellations and diversions involving Riyadh-bound services.
Abdul Alim, a Saudi expatriate from Comilla, was scheduled to depart for Riyadh on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight at 2am on Sunday.
He left home in the morning and reached Shahjalal International Airport around 8pm, only to find that his journey would not go ahead.
“The flight was at 2am, yet here I am, still waiting,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
Alim said passengers should have been informed earlier about the disruption, particularly as attacks and cancellations had already been reported over the preceding days.
“They could have informed us beforehand that the flight wouldn’t operate; instead, we have been subjected to this harassment,” he said.
But his greatest concern was not the hours spent waiting at the airport.
“I am now deeply worried; on one hand, there is the fear of losing my job with my employer in Saudi Arabia, and on the other, uncertainty about whether I will get a refund for the ticket or when I might be able to travel again.”
Ibrahim Molla, who travelled from Brahmanbaria for a Sunday night flight, expressed similar fears.
“My luck is bad; if I can’t leave now, I worry about how I will save my job. If I stay in the country, my wife and children will starve,” he said.
Their concerns were echoed by Shah Alam, another expatriate returning to Saudi Arabia after a holiday.
Despite purchasing his ticket in advance and arriving at the airport with his family, he learned that his flight had been cancelled.
He said he had received no clear information about when he could depart.
Any prolonged delay, he feared, could create problems with his employer, visa validity and conditions of employment.
A visit to Shahjalal International Airport found groups of expatriate passengers waiting outside Terminals 1 and 2.
Some had spent the entire night there after their flights were cancelled. Others were seeking information from airlines or preparing to return home.
Manik, who travelled from Chandpur to see off his brother Mobarak, said they arrived on Sunday evening only to discover that the flight would not operate.
After spending the night alternately standing and sitting outside the terminal, they finally decided to return home on Monday morning.
For passengers travelling from districts outside Dhaka, the cancellations have also meant additional transport costs, accommodation difficulties and uncertainty over whether they will have to make another journey to the capital.
State Minister for Civil Aviation and Tourism M Rashiduzzaman Millat said that the government was taking steps to reduce the financial and employment-related difficulties facing stranded passengers.
Speaking after a meeting with representatives of domestic and international airlines at the Secretariat, he said instructions had been issued to reissue tickets without cancellation fees.
The minister said arrangements were also being made for passengers whose Saudi visas were approaching expiry.
“Arrangements are being made to send those whose visa validity is expiring to Saudi Arabia via special flights from Medina and Dammam airports,” he said.
Earlier in the day, the minister cited the cancellation of 10 flights affecting 3,431 passengers. CAAB subsequently reported 12 cancellations by Monday afternoon.
The proposed alternative flights could offer relief to workers facing immediate deadlines, although detailed schedules and eligibility arrangements have yet to be announced.
The aviation crisis has unfolded alongside growing concern for Bangladeshis caught in the attack on Riyadh airport.
The foreign ministry identified the two deceased Bangladeshis as Md Shahed Ahmed and Md Nasrullah Badarpuri.
According to information received from the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh, another 24 Bangladeshis were injured.
Of them, 11 were employed in Saudi Arabia, while 13 had travelled to the kingdom on Umrah visas.
The injured were receiving treatment at hospitals in Riyadh, with embassy officials maintaining contact with hospital authorities to obtain updates and ensure necessary assistance.
Approximately 500 Bangladeshi passengers were also reported stranded at Riyadh airport amid the suspension of operations.
Saturday’s attack, attributed to Houthi rebels, has disrupted one of Saudi Arabia’s major international aviation hubs and complicated travel arrangements for thousands of passengers.
For Bangladesh, where large numbers of workers depend on employment in Saudi Arabia, the consequences are particularly serious.
While the government explores alternative routes and airlines prepare revised schedules, stranded passengers remain uncertain about when they can return to work, and whether their employers will wait for them.

item.title: Schools for all, but not for children with disabilities
item.description:
Farshad Ahmed’s family has spent nearly two decades searching for a school that could accommodate his learning needs.
Now, after repeated rejections, unsuccessful school transfers and years of frustration, they are considering leaving Khulna for Dhaka.
Farshad, in his early twenties, has Down syndrome.
His experience reflects a wider failure of Bangladesh’s education system, where children with intellectual and developmental disabilities continue to face exclusion despite legal protections, government commitments and a national framework for inclusive education.
Government schools often lack trained teachers and appropriate learning support, specialised education remains prohibitively expensive, and even the authorities acknowledge gaps in early identification.
The problem extends beyond classrooms.
Government agencies lack effective coordination, while officials and educators disagree over whether children with special educational needs require a separate curriculum or individualised support within mainstream education.
According to the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, 5.2% of children aged two to 17 have a functional difficulty in at least one domain.
Yet families say finding suitable education remains a struggle, particularly outside major cities.
Farshad’s family first attempted to enrol him at six. Several kindergartens and private schools refused admission.
One school eventually accepted him, but he struggled to adjust. His family changed schools four or five times.
“He could not keep pace with everyone else. Other children did not want to mix with him and drew a kind of boundary,” his sister Urnisha told Dhaka Tribune.
Eventually, Farshad became so frustrated that he cried and refused to attend school.
A specialised school offered little improvement. Children with different disabilities and widely varying ages were taught together without adequate individual support.
Home tutoring was another option, but trained educators were difficult to find and expensive.
His mother, Jebunnesa, said the family was considering relocating to Dhaka, where organisations supporting people with Down syndrome could offer better opportunities.
“It is hard to uproot everything, but we are thinking of our child’s future,” she said.
Teachers at a government primary school in Chandpur’s Faridganj upazila described similar difficulties.
They said children with disabilities were expected to follow the same curriculum as their classmates, often without the additional support they needed. Many eventually dropped out.
Department of Social Services figures show 4,046,520 registered persons with disabilities nationwide.
Among them, 209,938 have autism, intellectual disability, cerebral palsy or Down syndrome.
However, activists believe the actual number is substantially higher because many families never complete official registration.
Of 10 families of people with neurodevelopmental disabilities interviewed by Dhaka Tribune, eight had never registered for the government’s Suborno disability identity card.
Shah Mohammad Mahbub, director general of the Department of Social Services, acknowledged that early identification remains a major weakness.
“Early identification is very important, but at the moment we do not have the opportunity or specific tools for it,” he said.
Currently, registration depends on applications supported by medical certificates.
Without effective identification, many children risk missing educational support from an early age.
The government’s approach to inclusive education has also exposed differences among policymakers.
Md Joynal Abedin, additional director of the Inclusive Education Cell, said there would be no separate curriculum for children with special educational needs.
Instead, the general curriculum would be supported by more inclusive teaching methods.
“Our approach to inclusive pedagogy must change,” he said, warning that without changes in attitudes, inclusion would remain confined to policy documents.
However, State Minister for Health Dr M A Muhit, who also convenes the parliamentary caucus on disability rights, argued that standard textbooks cannot meet every child’s needs.
He advocated individualised education plans (IEPs), allowing teaching to be adapted to each student’s abilities.
Children with mild or moderate disabilities could learn in mainstream classrooms with appropriate support, he said, while those requiring intensive assistance needed specialised education.
Tahmina Parvin, acting head teacher of Ramna School for Intellectual Disabilities and Autism, called for a common national framework covering specialised education.
She also recommended dedicated recruitment of special educators in primary schools.
Although the government published its Special Education Needs and Disability Framework in December 2022 with Unicef support, implementation remains limited.
Fifty-two schools operated by SWID Bangladesh function under the Ministry of Social Welfare rather than the Ministry of Education, illustrating the fragmented administration of specialised education.
For many parents, financial hardship is as significant as the absence of suitable schools.
Specialised schools in Dhaka typically charge Tk20,000–Tk50,000 in monthly tuition, with admission fees ranging from Tk80,000 to Tk2 lakh.
At Vision Global, parents pay Tk1.65 lakh for admission and Tk40,000 monthly for a child requiring a shadow teacher, compared with less than Tk15,000 in tuition for other students.
Medical expenses add to the burden. The Health and Morbidity Status Survey 2025 found that persons with disabilities spent an average of Tk6,775 on treatment over the preceding 90 days.
For Shiuli Rahman of Azimpur, even transporting her 12-year-old autistic son, Abdur Rahman Shahriar, to an NGO-run school is a struggle.
Her husband died several years ago, and the daily journey costs at least Tk400.
“I cannot take him every day because of money,” she said. “I take him three days a week, when I have money in hand.”
Outside Dhaka, the shortage of specialised facilities makes the situation even more difficult.
Dr Shaoli Sarker, associate professor of neurology at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, said its Child Development Centre hears from at least six or seven families daily who cannot find appropriate schools.
Bangladesh’s disability rights legislation and international commitments recognise inclusive education, but advocates say implementation remains inadequate.
Rasheda K Chowdhury, executive director of the Campaign for Popular Education, said coordination among the education, social welfare, health and women and children affairs ministries was “completely absent”.
State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj acknowledged the importance of early identification, trained teachers, accessible schools and suitable learning materials.
“We are working on it,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
Experts recommend recruiting at least one specially trained teacher in every primary school, preparing individualised learning plans and bringing specialised schools under the Ministry of Education.
There are examples of what sustained support can achieve. Munni Sultana’s autistic son changed schools at least five times but is now a third-year student at Dhaka University.
For families like Farshad’s, however, access to education still depends heavily on where they live, what they can afford and whether a school is willing and equipped to accept their child.

item.title: Bangladesh embassy urges expatriates in Saudi Arabia to remain alert
item.description:
The Embassy of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh in Riyadh has urged expatriate Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia to remain alert amid the ongoing situation in the Middle East and follow safety and legal instructions issued by Saudi Arabian authorities.
The embassy issued the advisory in an emergency notice on Sunday.
According to the notice, recording, storing, sharing or posting information, photos or videos related to the situation in the Middle East on social media platforms, including Facebook, YouTube and X, formerly Twitter, is punishable under Saudi law.
The embassy urged expatriates to comply with Saudi law and refrain from sharing or circulating such images, videos and sensitive information.
It also advised them to avoid high-risk and crowded areas and take necessary precautions while following instructions issued by Saudi authorities.
For urgent assistance, expatriate Bangladeshis can contact the embassy through its hotlines. Calls to 8001000125 for labour-related matters and 8001000126 for passport-related services are free of charge. The hotline for diplomatic wing-related matters is 8001000124.
For emergencies involving deaths, expatriates can call +966570212180.
The embassy also advised expatriates to follow its verified Facebook page for regular and reliable updates on the situation in the Middle East.

item.title: Chawkbazar fire rages on after 5 hours, 10 units deployed
item.description:
Five hours after a fire broke out at a multi-storey building in Old Dhaka’s Chawkbazar on Monday evening, the blaze remained uncontrolled, with 10 Fire Service and Civil Defence units working to extinguish it.
The fire broke out at a shop on the sixth floor of Mansur Khan Plaza, beside AC Mosque in the Chhota Katra area, at 5:02pm.
Fire engines from the nearest fire station were dispatched at 5:04pm, but the first unit reached the scene at 5:22pm after navigating traffic and narrow lanes. The station is about two kilometres from the building.
Fire Service officials at the scene said the lack of an immediate water source in the densely populated area of Old Dhaka was making firefighting difficult.
Firefighters are trying to extinguish the blaze by extending hoses from distant water sources and using water tankers.
The cause of the fire and any casualties have yet to be reported.

item.title: ‘My 2am flight never took off; I’m still at Dhaka airport’
item.description:
Abdul Alim had set out from Comilla early in the morning, hoping to catch a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight to Riyadh, the Saudi capital, scheduled to depart at 2:00am on Monday. By 8:00pm, he had reached Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, expecting to begin his journey.
But he never got to board it.
“My flight was at 2:00am, and I’m still sitting here,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
Alim said several flights had already been cancelled over the past three days, leaving many passengers stranded.
“If we had been informed beforehand that the flight would not operate, we could have avoided this. Instead, we had to go through all this harassment,” he said.
The disruption has also left him worried about his job in Saudi Arabia, his ticket refund and when he will be able to travel. “I’m extremely worried. On one hand, I fear losing my job in Saudi Arabia. On the other, I don’t know whether I’ll get a refund for my ticket or when I’ll be able to fly,” he said.
Brahmanbaria resident Ibrahim Molla was similarly stranded after arriving at the airport on Sunday evening for his flight. “My luck is bad. Now I’m worried about how I’ll save my job if I cannot return. If I stay in Bangladesh, my wife and children will have nothing to eat,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
After visiting Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, it was found that scores of expatriate passengers waiting outside Terminals-1 and 2 after their Riyadh-bound flights were cancelled.
Repeated cancellations since Saturday have left passengers crowding the terminals, with some waiting for updates and others returning home after spending hours at the airport.
Manik from Chandpur told Dhaka Tribune that he had travelled to Dhaka with his brother Mobarak, whom he had accompanied to the airport. They arrived on Sunday evening but later learned that the flight had been cancelled.
“We waited at the airport until dawn before returning home in the morning,” he said.
Another Saudi-bound passenger, Shah Alam, said he was scheduled to return to Saudi Arabia on Sunday night after spending his leave in Bangladesh.
He had purchased his ticket in advance and arrived at the airport with his family at the scheduled time, only to learn that his flight had been cancelled.
He said he had not received clear information about when the next flight would depart.
“I have to return to Saudi Arabia at any cost. I will face problems if I cannot reach there on time,” he said.
He added that he was worried about losing his job or facing problems over his visa and employer’s requirements if he failed to report to work on time.
Fifty-one flights from Dhaka to Riyadh have been cancelled since the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital, according to the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB).
The cancelled flights were scheduled to carry a total of 5,418 passengers, CAAB said on Monday afternoon.
Among direct flights, a total of 12 were disrupted, four operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, two by US-Bangla Airlines, three by Saudia Airlines and three by Riyadh Air.
Another 39 transit flights were disrupted, including 16 operated by IndiGo Airlines, three by SalamAir, one by EgyptAir, nine by Emirates, five by Qatar Airways and five by flydubai.
Overall, 51 flights were affected, 12 direct and 39 transit flights, disrupting travel for a total of 5,418 passengers.
Operations at King Khalid International Airport were suspended after the attack on Saturday night, disrupting air connectivity between Dhaka and Riyadh.
Passengers have been advised to contact their respective airlines for the latest updates on their flights.
According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, all flights bound for Riyadh were either diverted or cancelled following the Houthi attack and explosions at the airport on Sunday, Reuters reported.
Reuters also reported that airport authorities had advised passengers to contact their airlines before travelling to the airport and verify the latest status of their flights.
CAAB Assistant Director (Public Relations) Muhammad Kawsar Mahmud told Dhaka Tribune on Monday afternoon that 12 flights had been cancelled, affecting more than 4,000 passengers and expatriate Bangladeshis.
“Depending on the situation, the airlines will announce the schedules of subsequent flights. We have advised passengers to remain in contact with their airlines,” he said.
Two Bangladeshis were killed and 24 others injured in the attack, while around 500 Bangladeshi passengers remain stranded due to the disruption to flight operations.
According to sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, the two deceased were Md Shahed Ahmed and Md Nasrullah Badrpuri.
Citing the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh, the Foreign Ministry said 11 of the 24 injured Bangladeshis were Saudi-based workers, while the other 13 had travelled to the country on Umrah visas.
They are receiving treatment at various hospitals in Riyadh. The Bangladesh Embassy is maintaining contact with hospital authorities to gather information about the injured and ensure they receive necessary treatment.
On Saturday, Houthi rebels launched a drone attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Following the attack, all operations at the airport were suspended indefinitely.
The suspension has left Bangladeshi expatriates and Umrah pilgrims facing severe travel disruptions.
The attack is reportedly the deadliest assault in a Gulf Arab country since the Iran-US war began in February.

item.title: Riyadh airport extends suspension after attacks
item.description:
Saudi authorities on Monday extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh’s international airport following a series of deadly Houthi attacks.
Strikes on the airport last week killed at least 18 people, including 13 on Saturday in the deadliest attack on the country in more than a decade, which also left hundreds wounded.
The General Authority of Civil Aviation in a statement “announced the extension of the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport.”
It said the extension was needed to “complete the necessary procedures to verify the safety of the facilities and their operational readiness.”
The authority did not specify when operations would resume.
A senior aviation source who oversees flights to the Gulf for an airline said operations would be halted for the remainder of the working week in Saudi Arabia, according to messages sent to the carrier on Monday from Saudi aviation authorities.
“They told us it would be until at least Thursday. There are no flights until the end of the week,” the source told AFP.
A senior official from the Riyadh Metro also told AFP that authorities had suspended transport services to three stations serving the airport.

item.title: Music artist Rushnaf Wadud passes away
item.description:
Rushnaf Wadud, a prominent figure in Bangladesh’s independent music scene and the lead vocalist of alternative rock band Blunderware, died of heart attack on Monday.
The news of his death was confirmed by his friend and longtime bandmate Moktadir Dewan.
Rushnaf had also been dealing with long-standing respiratory complications.
Known for his distinctive vocal delivery, thoughtful songwriting and experimental musical style, Rushnaf was among the familiar names in Bangladesh’s independent music scene, where he developed a reputation for blending alternative rock with folk-inspired sounds.
He rose to prominence as the frontman of Blunderware, a band known for its unconventional musical approach and layered lyrics. One of the group’s best-known tracks, 'Afim Chaash', showcased its distinctive blend of indie rock, folk and blues influences. The song was written by Rushnaf and composed by Blunderware.
Rushnaf was also associated with The Attempted Band, where he served as lead vocalist. Songs including 'Ei Bikale' and 'O Moushumi' were among the tracks associated with his musical journey.
Beyond music, Rushnaf also explored acting, appearing in the critically acclaimed Bangladeshi anthology film 'Sincerely Yours, Dhaka', released in 2019. The film brought together multiple stories set in the capital, reflecting different aspects of urban life.
His death has prompted an outpouring of grief among musicians, filmmakers and listeners, many of whom remember him for his creativity, collaborative spirit and contribution to the country’s independent music culture.
Rushnaf’s passing marks a loss for a music scene in which he carved out a distinctive space through his voice, songwriting and commitment to artistic experimentation.

item.title: Saudi restrictions affect 51 flights at Dhaka airport
item.description:

item.title: Dengue cases surpass 100,000 this year
item.description:
The number of dengue cases in Bangladesh has surpassed 100,000 this year, with 2,167 new patients hospitalized in the 24 hours until 8:00am on Monday.
During the period, four people died of the mosquito-borne disease, taking the death toll in the country to 307 this year.
All four deaths were reported in the Dhaka South City Corporation area, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Since January 1 this year, a total of 1,01,442 dengue patients have been admitted to hospitals across the country. Of them, 95,331 have recovered.

item.title: Shama: Bangladesh ready to help protect Mecca, Medina
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Monday said Bangladesh would extend necessary assistance to Saudi Arabia if the holy cities of Mecca and Medina faced any security threat amid the ongoing regional conflict.
"If any threat emerges against Mecca or Medina, Bangladesh will certainly not remain indifferent. We will extend a helping hand to protect the two holy cities," she told journalists.
The state minister made the remarks after attending a seminar titled "Foreign Policy of Bangladesh: Navigating Pathways in a Shifting World", organised by the Bangladesh Institute of International and Strategic Studies (BIISS) in Dhaka.
Responding to a question about Bangladesh's willingness to assist Saudi Arabia in safeguarding the two holy cities, Shama said the issue carried deep religious and emotional significance for Muslims worldwide.
"For Muslims, Mecca and Medina are not merely matters of diplomacy. They are also deeply connected to our emotions and religious sentiments," she said.
She continued that Bangladesh, as a Muslim-majority country, shared the concerns of Muslims across the world regarding the security of the two holy cities.
The state minister, however, clarified that Bangladesh had not yet formally joined the proposed Mecca Pact.
"We have not yet joined the Mecca Pact. A decision can be considered final only when the process is formally completed," she said.
Responding to a question about the possibility of sending Bangladeshi troops to Saudi Arabia under the proposed arrangement, Shama said the issue did not arise at present.
"Since Bangladesh has not joined the Mecca Pact, the question of sending troops under that arrangement does not arise at this moment," she said.
Her remarks came against the backdrop of repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport.
Bangladesh has strongly condemned the attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure and expressed solidarity with the Saudi government and people.
Shama said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had also sent a letter to the Saudi crown prince conveying Bangladesh's position.
"We want an immediate end to these attacks. We stand beside the people and government of Saudi Arabia," she said.
The state minister reiterated Bangladesh's call for an end to hostilities, saying continued violence was claiming innocent lives and threatening regional stability.
The BIISS seminar featured presentations by Ayesha Binte Towhid on national interest-driven foreign policy, Dr Mahfuz Kabir on economic priorities, ASM Tarek Hassan Semul on defence and security, and Dr Sufia Khanom on ideological interests in foreign policy.
BIISS Director General Major General ASM Ridwanur Rahman delivered the welcome address and chaired the session.

item.title: MES praises Walton’s technological manufacturing strength
item.description:
A high-level delegation of the Military Engineer Services (MES) visited the headquarters of Walton Hi-Tech Industries PLC at Chandra, Gazipur, and expressed admiration for the company’s vast manufacturing scale, advanced technologies, research and development activities, product diversity and international-standard production capabilities.
The delegation was led by Major General Hasan Uz Zaman, engineer-in-chief of the Military Engineer Services.
Other members of the delegation included Brigadier General Abul Hasnat Mohammad Sayem, director, Works, along with senior officials of MES.
During the recent visit, the MES delegation was welcomed by SM Mahbubul Alam, managing director of Walton Hi-Tech Industries PLC, along with other senior officials of the company.
Members of the delegation visited Walton’s display centre, various production plants, and research and innovation activities.
They observed the manufacturing processes and technological excellence of a wide range of electrical, electronic and hi-tech products, including lifts, air conditioners, refrigerators, solar panels, batteries, cables and compressors.
Major General Hasan Uz Zaman said: “We are truly impressed by Walton’s vast manufacturing scale, product diversity and technological capabilities. In particular, the company’s research and development activities are highly commendable. We would like to see Walton further expand these capabilities and continue advancing in technological innovation.”
Emphasizing the importance of prioritizing locally manufactured products, he said: “Like the government, we also place importance on giving preference to products made in Bangladesh. If the required products are available locally, we would first consider locally manufactured products. In this regard, Walton is one of the companies that naturally comes to our consideration. Its contribution to industrialization, employment generation, local manufacturing, technological development and the national economy truly deserves appreciation.”
Brigadier General Abul Hasnat Mohammad Sayem, director, Works of the Military Engineer Services, said: “Walton’s extensive manufacturing capability is truly remarkable. It is a matter of great pride that such large-scale manufacturing facilities and industrial capabilities have been developed in Bangladesh, and products manufactured here are being exported to different countries around the world.”
SM Mahbubul Alam, managing director of Walton Hi-Tech Industries PLC, said: “Walton places great importance on building long-term cooperation with key national institutions based on technology and manufacturing capabilities. The visit of the Military Engineer Services delegation is highly significant for us. Their valuable observations and recommendations will inspire us to further advance local technology-product manufacturing, research and development.”
Tanvir Anjum, business coordinator to the managing director of Walton Hi-Tech Industries PLC and senior executive director of the company, oversees Walton’s business activities, communication and coordination with MES.
He hosted the program and expressed sincere gratitude to the MES delegation for their visit.
Among others present during the visit were Mohammad Yusuf Ali, additional managing director of Walton; Md Tanvir Rahman, chief business officer of Walton AC; Ahmad Tanvir, head of corporate sales; Protic Kumar Modak, senior executive director; Md Mahmudur Rahman, CBO of Walton Lift; and Tanvir Ahmad, head of admin, along with other officials.
